relationship: parallel manifestation of God's salvation and mercy
rationale: Isaiah announces the nearness of God's salvation and the revealing of His mercy; the psalm declares His salvation made known and His mercy remembered toward Jacob. The announcement and the psalm's accomplished acts have different time frames.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “Keep justice; do righteousness. For the coming of My salvation has drawn near, and the revealing of My mercy.

target_units.text: The Lord made His salvation known; before the nations He revealed His righteousness.
He remembered His mercy to Jacob and His truth to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God.

relationship: legal counterpart to keeping the Sabbath from profanation
rationale: Isaiah blesses the person who keeps the Sabbaths from profanation; Exodus commands remembering the Sabbath and keeping it holy through cessation of work. Isaiah also requires guarding the hands from wrongdoing.
source_text: Happy is the man who does these things, the person holding fast to them, keeping the Sabbaths from profanation and guarding his hands from wrongdoing.”

target_units.text: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
For six days you shall labour and do all your works;

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it: you, and your son, and your daughter, your male slave, and your female slave, your ox, and your beast of burden, and all your livestock, and the resident foreigner who dwells with you.
For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.

relationship: contrast between exclusion from the assembly and the eunuch's promised belonging
rationale: Deuteronomy excludes a man with crushed testicles or a cut-off organ from the Lord's assembly; Isaiah tells the eunuch not to call himself a dry tree, before promising faithful eunuchs a place in God's house. The physical descriptions and covenantal settings are preserved rather than treated as identical wording.
source_text: Let no foreigner attached to the Lord say, “Will the Lord then separate me from His people?” And let no eunuch say, “I am a dry tree.”

target_units.text: He whose testicles are crushed, or whose organ is cut off, shall not enter the assembly of the Lord.

relationship: parallel faithfulness of eunuchs before the Lord
rationale: Isaiah names eunuchs who keep the Sabbaths, choose God's wishes and hold His covenant; Wisdom describes a eunuch whose hand does no lawless deed and who conceives no evil against the Lord. Their particular duties differ, while faithfulness defines the favorable description in both.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths, choose what I wish, and hold fast to My covenant,

target_units.text: and the eunuch who has done no lawless deed with his hand and has not conceived evil against the Lord; for a choice favor will be given him for his faithfulness, and a more delightful portion in the Lord’s temple.

relationship: close honored portion in God's house for a faithful eunuch
rationale: Isaiah promises a renowned place in God's house and wall, better than sons and daughters; Wisdom promises the faithful eunuch a choice favor and delightful portion in the Lord's temple. Isaiah expressly adds an everlasting name, which Wisdom's individual verse does not state.
source_text: I will give them in My house and wall a renowned place better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it will not fail.

target_units.text: and the eunuch who has done no lawless deed with his hand and has not conceived evil against the Lord; for a choice favor will be given him for his faithfulness, and a more delightful portion in the Lord’s temple.

relationship: parallel foreigners serving the God whose name is over the temple
rationale: Isaiah welcomes foreigners attached to the Lord and loving His name; Solomon's prayer asks God to hear foreigners praying toward the house so all peoples may know and fear His name. Isaiah specifically requires Sabbath observance and covenant fidelity.
source_text: And the foreigners attached to the Lord, to serve Him and love the Lord’s name, to become His male and female slaves, and all those keeping My Sabbaths from profanation and holding fast to My covenant—

target_units.text: “Also concerning the foreigner who is not of Thy people,
when they come and pray toward this place,

hear from heaven, from Thy prepared dwelling place, and do all that the foreigner calls upon Thee for, so that all the peoples may know Thy name and fear Thee as Thy people Israel do, and may know that Thy name is called over this house I have built.

relationship: explicit citation of the house of prayer for all nations
rationale: Mark introduces Jesus' temple saying as written Scripture and repeats the house of prayer for all nations. The subsequent accusation of a robbers' den is additional to this Isaiah unit.
source_text: I will bring them into My holy mountain and make them rejoice in My house of prayer. Their whole burnt offerings and sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations,”

target_units.text: He taught and said to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.”

relationship: explicit house-of-prayer citation in the temple
rationale: Matthew records Jesus saying that it is written that His house will be called a house of prayer. The citation preserves that clause while not repeating Isaiah's express phrase for all nations.
source_text: I will bring them into My holy mountain and make them rejoice in My house of prayer. Their whole burnt offerings and sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations,”

target_units.text: He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a robbers’ cave.”

relationship: explicit house-of-prayer citation during the temple action
rationale: Luke records the scriptural saying that God's house shall be a house of prayer as Jesus drives sellers out. Its cited wording does not repeat Isaiah's sacrifices, holy mountain or all-nations clause.
source_text: I will bring them into My holy mountain and make them rejoice in My house of prayer. Their whole burnt offerings and sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations,”

target_units.text: saying to them, “It is written, ‘And My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.”

relationship: close gathering of Israel's dispersed people
rationale: Isaiah identifies the Lord as the One gathering Israel's scattered people and promises a gathering; the psalm likewise says the Lord will gather Israel's dispersed people as He builds Jerusalem.
source_text: said the Lord who gathers Israel’s scattered people, “for I will gather a gathering to him.”

target_units.text: The Lord builds Jerusalem, and He will gather the dispersed of Israel.

relationship: close summons for wild beasts to gather and eat
rationale: Isaiah summons wild beasts and woodland beasts to come and eat; Jeremiah summons the field's wild beasts to gather and eat God's abandoned inheritance. Jeremiah names the object of the eating, which this Isaiah summons leaves unstated.
source_text: All you wild beasts, come and eat, all you beasts of the woodland!

target_units.text: Is My inheritance to Me a hyena’s cave, or a cave around her? Go, gather all the field’s wild beasts, and let them come to eat her!

relationship: analogy between mute dogs and a watchman's failed warning
rationale: Isaiah portrays blind, unthinking figures as dogs unable to bark and loving to doze; Ezekiel describes a watchman who sees an approaching sword but fails to sound the trumpet. The failed audible warning is the comparison, without identifying the two figures as the same office.
source_text: See: all have been blinded; they did not know how to think. They are all mute dogs, unable to bark, dreaming of a bed, loving to doze.

target_units.text: If the watchman sees the sword coming but does not signal with the trumpet, and the people do not take care, and the sword comes and takes a life from them, that life was taken because of its own lawlessness, but I will require the blood from the watchman’s hand.’

relationship: related rebuke of self-serving appetite
rationale: Isaiah condemns insatiable dogs who each follow their own ways; Ezekiel rebukes shepherds consuming milk, clothing themselves with wool and slaughtering fattened animals while not feeding God's sheep. The rebukes use different animal images and roles to expose appetite directed toward oneself.
source_text: The dogs are shameless in appetite, knowing no satisfaction, and they are evil, without understanding. They all followed their own ways, each according to what was his own.

target_units.text: “Son of man, prophesy against Israel’s shepherds. Prophesy and say to the shepherds, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O shepherds of Israel, surely shepherds do not feed themselves? Do shepherds not feed the sheep?
Behold, you consume the milk, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the fattened animal, but you do not feed My sheep.

relationship: close removal of a righteous person from wickedness misunderstood by observers
rationale: Isaiah says a righteous person was taken from injustice while no one understands or takes it to heart; Wisdom describes the pleasing person removed from wickedness while observers neither understand nor consider it. Wisdom develops the protective purpose of the removal.
source_text: See how the righteous man perished, and no one considers it in his heart. Righteous men are removed, and no one understands. For the righteous man was taken from the presence of injustice.

target_units.text: Having become pleasing to God, he was loved, and while living among sinners he was transferred.
He was snatched away, lest evil change his understanding or deceit mislead his soul;
for the fascination of wickedness obscures what is good, and the wandering of desire alters an innocent mind.
Having been brought to completion in a short time, he fulfilled long years;
for his soul was pleasing to the Lord; therefore he hastened from the midst of wickedness. Yet the peoples saw and did not understand, nor set such a thing in their minds:

relationship: parallel peace of the righteous after apparent loss
rationale: Isaiah says the righteous person's burial will be in peace; Wisdom says the righteous seem to have suffered destruction in their departure but are in peace. The target discusses their souls in God's hand rather than the burial itself.
source_text: His burial will be in peace; he has been removed from the midst.

target_units.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and torment will surely not touch them.
In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was reckoned a calamity,
and their going away from us a destruction; but they are in peace.

relationship: close address to children of prostitution
rationale: Isaiah calls the hearers offspring of adulterers and a prostitute; Hosea names children of prostitution and describes their mother's adultery and pursuit of lovers. The familial sexual imagery marks the communities' unfaithfulness in both settings.
source_text: “But you, come forward here, lawless sons, offspring of adulterers and a prostitute!

target_units.text: “Enter into judgment with your mother, enter into judgment! For she is not My wife and I am not her husband. I will remove her prostitution from My face and her adultery from between her breasts,
so that I may strip her naked and restore her as on the day of her birth. I will make her like a wilderness, set her like a waterless land and kill her with thirst.
I will certainly show no mercy to her children, for they are children of prostitution.

For their mother prostituted herself; she who bore them brought shame. She said, ‘I will follow my lovers, who give me my loaves and water, my garments and linen cloths, my oil and everything due to me.’

relationship: related hostile opening of the mouth
rationale: Isaiah challenges the hearers' opened mouths and loosened tongues; the psalm portrays assailants opening their mouths like a roaring, predatory lion. The psalm speaks from the afflicted person's position, while Isaiah addresses the aggressors.
source_text: In whom did you delight? Against whom did you open your mouth and let loose your tongue? Are you not children of destruction, lawless offspring?

target_units.text: They opened their mouth against me like a lion seizing prey and roaring.

relationship: parallel condemnation of child sacrifice in a ravine
rationale: Isaiah condemns slaughtering children in ravines among rocks while appealing to idols; Jeremiah names Topheth in Hinnom's ravine, where children were burned contrary to God's command. Jeremiah specifies the location and method more narrowly than Isaiah's unit does.
source_text: You who appeal to idols beneath leafy trees, slaughtering their children in ravines among the rocks!

target_units.text: And they built Topheth’s altar, which is in the ravine of the son of Hinnom, to burn up their sons and daughters in fire, which I did not command them and did not conceive in My heart.

relationship: close illicit libations provoking divine anger
rationale: Isaiah recounts libations and sacrifices to the objects of the preceding accusation and asks whether God will be angry; Jeremiah describes drink offerings to foreign gods to provoke Him to anger. Jeremiah also describes the shame returning upon the worshipers.
source_text: That is your portion; this is your lot. To those you poured libations, and to those you brought sacrifices. Will I not therefore be angry over these things?

target_units.text: Their sons gather wood, and their fathers burn a fire, and their women work dough to make cakes for heaven’s host; and they poured drink offerings to foreign gods to provoke Me to anger.
Is it Me they provoke to anger? says the Lord. Is it not themselves, so that their faces are put to shame?

relationship: parallel sacrifices on elevated places amid sexual unfaithfulness
rationale: Isaiah places a bed and sacrifices on a high mountain; Hosea describes sacrifices on mountaintops and hills within its account of prostitution and adultery. Hosea additionally names sheltering trees, while Isaiah's unit emphasizes the elevated bed.
source_text: On a high and lofty mountain—there is your bed, and there you brought sacrifices up.

target_units.text: On the mountaintops they sacrificed, and on the hills they offered sacrifice, beneath oak, poplar and a tree providing shade, because shelter is good. Therefore your daughters will prostitute themselves and your daughters-in-law commit adultery.

relationship: related bed imagery for unfaithfulness with foreign lovers
rationale: Isaiah accuses the addressee of departure from God and loving those who sleep with her; Ezekiel describes Babylon's sons coming to Jerusalem's personification and a bed of lodgers in prostitution. The target does not reproduce Isaiah's memorials behind doorposts.
source_text: Behind your doorposts you set your memorials. You thought that if you departed from Me you would have something more. You loved those sleeping with you

target_units.text: Babylon’s sons came to her, to a bed of lodgers, and defiled her in her prostitution. She was defiled by them, and her soul withdrew from them.

relationship: close sending of distant messengers in an account of prostitution
rationale: Isaiah joins multiplied prostitution with ambassadors sent beyond the boundaries; Ezekiel says the personified city desired the depicted Chaldeans and sent messengers to their land. Isaiah additionally describes humiliation as far as Hades.
source_text: and multiplied your prostitution with them. You increased the number of those far away from you, sent ambassadors beyond your boundaries, turned away, and were humbled as far as Hades.

target_units.text: She set her desire upon them at the sight of her eyes and sent messengers to them in the Chaldeans’ land.

relationship: related persistence in exhausting pursuit of strangers
rationale: Isaiah describes weariness from many journeys without saying to stop and continuing to strengthen oneself; Jeremiah tells the woman to turn from a rough road and thirst, but she says she will be strong and follows strangers. The surrounding accounts concern unfaithful pursuit.
source_text: You wore yourself out with your many journeys and did not say, ‘I will stop.’ You kept strengthening yourself because you did these things; therefore you did not implore Me—

target_units.text: Turn your foot from a rough road and your throat from thirst. But she said, I will be strong, because she had loved strangers and went after them.

relationship: internal connection between misplaced fear and forgetting God
rationale: Isaiah 57 asks whom the hearers feared so that they lied and forgot God; Isaiah 51 names fear of a mortal oppressor and forgetting the Creator. The latter identifies the feared person more specifically.
source_text: you! Whom did you reverently fear, that you lied to Me, did not remember Me, and took Me neither into thought nor into your heart? I see you and overlook you, yet you did not fear Me.

target_units.text: “I am, I am the One comforting you. Recognize whom you dreaded and feared: a mortal person, a human being who withered like grass.

You forgot God who made you, who made heaven and founded earth, and feared continually, every day, the face of your oppressor’s anger. For as he planned to remove you—where now is your oppressor’s anger?

relationship: close challenge that chosen gods should rescue their worshipers
rationale: Isaiah challenges the objects of reliance to rescue the hearers in distress; Judges tells Israel, which abandoned the Lord for other gods, to cry to those gods for rescue in affliction. Isaiah also predicts their removal by wind and storm.
source_text: When you cry aloud, let them rescue you in your distress! Wind will take all these, and a storm carry them away. But those holding fast to Me will acquire land and inherit My holy mountain.

target_units.text: But you have forsaken Me and served other gods. Therefore I will save you no more.
Go and cry to the gods which you have chosen for yourselves; let them save you in the time of your affliction.”

relationship: parallel land inheritance for those holding to the Lord
rationale: Isaiah promises land and God's holy mountain to those holding fast to Him; the psalm promises land to those waiting for the Lord and to the meek. The holy mountain is specified only in Isaiah.
source_text: When you cry aloud, let them rescue you in your distress! Wind will take all these, and a storm carry them away. But those holding fast to Me will acquire land and inherit My holy mountain.

target_units.text: For those doing evil will be destroyed, but those who wait for the Lord will inherit the land.
A little longer, and the sinner will certainly not exist; you will seek his place and certainly not find it.
But the meek will inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace.

relationship: internal command to clear a road for God's people
rationale: Both command preparation of a road for God's people. Isaiah 57 names removing obstacles; Isaiah 62 names scattering stones from the road and raising a signal for nations.
source_text: They will say, ‘Clear roads before him, and remove obstacles from My people’s road.’

target_units.text: Go through My gates and make a road for My people. Scatter the stones from the road; raise a signal for the nations!

relationship: parallel divine help for the brokenhearted
rationale: Isaiah's exalted Lord gives life to the brokenhearted and patience to the fainthearted; the psalm says the Lord is near the brokenhearted and saves the humble in spirit. Isaiah locates His resting among holy ones, not explicitly among the brokenhearted.
source_text: Thus says the Lord Most High, who dwells in the heights for ever, whose name is Holy among holy ones, the Lord Most High resting among holy ones and giving patience to the fainthearted and life to the brokenhearted:

target_units.text: The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and He will save the humble in spirit.

relationship: close denial that divine anger lasts forever
rationale: Isaiah says God will not avenge forever or always be angry; the psalm says He will not remain angry to the end or maintain wrath forever. Isaiah additionally grounds the declaration in His making every breath.
source_text: ‘I will not take vengeance on you for ever or always be angry with you. For spirit will go out from Me, and I made every breath.

target_units.text: He will not be angry to the end, nor maintain wrath for ever.

relationship: close distress when God turns His face away
rationale: Isaiah describes God striking and turning His face away, followed by the person's grief and gloomy path; the psalmist says God turned His face away and he became troubled. Isaiah expressly names sin as the occasion.
source_text: Because of sin I grieved him a little, struck him, and turned My face away from him. He was grieved and went gloomily along his ways.

target_units.text: Lord, in Thy will Thou didst supply strength to my beauty; but Thou didst turn Thy face away, and I became troubled.

relationship: parallel God healing those in distress
rationale: Isaiah describes God seeing the person's ways, healing and comforting him after his grief; the psalm says He heals the brokenhearted and binds their fractures. The target supplies brokenheartedness and fracture imagery rather than Isaiah's repeated comfort.
source_text: I have seen his ways, healed him, comforted him, and given him true comfort—

target_units.text: He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their fractures.

relationship: close proclamation of peace to those far and near
rationale: Isaiah announces peace upon peace to those far away and near, with God's promise to heal; Ephesians says Christ proclaimed peace to those far away and those near. Its context explains their reconciliation and shared access to the Father.
source_text: peace upon peace to those far away and those near. And the Lord said, ‘I will heal them.’

target_units.text: And He came and proclaimed peace to you who were far away, and peace to those who were near,

relationship: related wave imagery of the ungodly
rationale: Isaiah's unjust are tossed by waves and unable to rest; Jude portrays the people it condemns as wild sea waves foaming up their own shames. Being tossed by waves and being compared to waves remain distinct formulations.
source_text: But the unjust will be tossed by waves in this way and will be unable to rest.

target_units.text: wild waves of the sea foaming up their own shames; wandering stars for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever.

relationship: internal repeated denial of rejoicing for the ungodly
rationale: Both conclude with the Lord's declaration that there is no rejoicing for the ungodly. The native wording is rejoicing in both passages, rather than a substituted peace formula.
source_text: ‘There is no rejoicing for the ungodly,’ said the Lord God.”

target_units.text: “There is no rejoicing for the ungodly,” says the Lord.

relationship: close announcement of Jacob's and Israel's sins
rationale: Isaiah commands loud proclamation of the people's sins and Jacob's lawless acts; Micah's passage connects strength in the Lord's Spirit with declaring Jacob's impieties and Israel's sins. Isaiah adds the trumpet comparison for the voice.
source_text: “Shout with strength and do not spare! Raise your voice like a trumpet and announce My people’s sins to them, and Jacob’s house their lawless acts.

target_units.text: unless I fill up strength in the Spirit of the Lord and of judgment and might, to declare to Jacob his impieties and to Israel his sins.”

relationship: related eagerness for God's words without corresponding conduct
rationale: Isaiah describes daily seeking of God and requests for righteous judgment before exposing oppressive fasting; Ezekiel describes people eagerly gathering to hear God's words but refusing to do them. The forms of apparent devotion differ.
source_text: Day after day they seek Me and desire to know My ways. Like a people who practiced righteousness and did not abandon their God’s judgment, they now ask Me righteous judgment and desire to draw near to God,

target_units.text: And you, son of man, your people’s sons talk about you beside the walls and in the houses’ gateways. A man says to his brother, ‘Let us gather and hear what comes from the Lord!’
They come to you as people assemble and sit before you. They hear your words but certainly will not do them, because falsehood is in their mouth, and their heart follows defilements.
You become to them like the sound of a sweet-voiced, well-tuned psaltery. They will hear your words but certainly will not do them.

relationship: close questioning of whether fasting is truly for God
rationale: Isaiah answers a complaint about unnoticed fasting by exposing pursuit of the fasters' wishes and pressure upon those under them; Zechariah asks whether the people's fast was for God and says they eat and drink for themselves. The shared issue is the practice's self-directed purpose.
source_text: saying, ‘Why did we fast, and Thou didst not see? We humbled our lives, and Thou didst not notice?’ For on your fasting days you pursue your wishes and prod all those under your control.

target_units.text: “Say to all the land’s people and to the priests: If you fast or mourn at the fifth or seventh observances—and look, seventy years—surely you have not fasted a fast for Me?
If you eat or drink, are you not yourselves eating and yourselves drinking?

relationship: related condemnation of fighting joined with corrupted devotion
rationale: Isaiah questions fasting used for disputes, fighting and striking a humble person; James connects fighting with pleasures and describes prayers that receive nothing because they serve those pleasures. James discusses asking rather than fasting.
source_text: If you fast for lawsuits and fights and strike a humble person with fists, why do you fast for Me as today, to make your voice heard in an outcry?

target_units.text: Where do wars come from, and where do fights among you come from? Is it not from here—from your pleasures that wage war in your members?
You desire and do not have; you murder and envy and cannot obtain. You fight and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.
You ask and do not receive, because you ask badly, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.

relationship: contrast between outward mourning gestures and heartfelt turning
rationale: Isaiah denies that a bent neck, sackcloth and ashes by themselves make an acceptable fast; Joel calls for fasting with the whole heart and tearing hearts rather than garments. Both resist reducing devotion to its visible gestures.
source_text: I did not choose this fast, or a day for a person to humble his life. Even if you bend your neck like a ring and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you, you will not thereby call it an acceptable fast.

target_units.text: “And now,” says the Lord your God, “turn to Me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning.”
Tear your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, because He is merciful and compassionate, patient and abundant in mercy, and relents concerning calamities.

relationship: related release of the oppressed as divinely appointed action
rationale: Isaiah's chosen fast releases the crushed and breaks unjust bonds and contracts; Jesus reads a mission including sending the oppressed away in release. Luke's wider Isaiah reading is not presented as a verbatim quotation of this entire fasting instruction.
source_text: ‘It is not such a fast that I chose,’ says the Lord. ‘Instead, loosen every bond of injustice, undo the strangling ties of coercive agreements, release the crushed, and tear up every unjust written contract.

target_units.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He anointed Me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed away in release,

relationship: parallel feeding, welcoming and clothing those in need
rationale: Isaiah commands bread for the hungry, shelter for homeless poor people and clothing for the naked; Matthew's King commends feeding, welcoming strangers and clothing, identifying care for His least brothers with care for Him. Isaiah also expressly names one's own family.
source_text: Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.

target_units.text: For I was hungry and you gave Me food, I was thirsty and you gave Me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed Me,
naked and you clothed Me, I was sick and you visited Me, I was in prison and you came to Me.’
Then the righteous will answer Him, ‘Lord, when did we see Thee hungry and feed Thee, or thirsty and give Thee drink?
When did we see Thee a stranger and welcome Thee, or naked and clothe Thee?
When did we see Thee sick or in prison and come to Thee?’
The King will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it to one of the least of these My brothers, you did it to Me.’

relationship: practical counterpart to providing food and clothing
rationale: Isaiah commands actual food and clothing for those lacking them; James rejects a peaceful wish that supplies neither clothing nor daily food and calls faith without works dead. The target explicitly tests a claim to faith through those concrete provisions.
source_text: Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.

target_units.text: If a brother or sister is without clothing and lacks daily food,
and one of you says to them, “Go in peace; be warmed and filled,” but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it?
So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead by itself.

relationship: internal restored light accompanied by God's glory
rationale: Isaiah 58 promises light breaking out and God's glory enfolding the merciful hearer; Isaiah 60 tells Jerusalem to shine because her light has come and God's glory has risen upon her. The settings share light and divine glory with different descriptions of their arrival.
source_text: Then your light will break out early, and your healings quickly rise. Your righteousness will go ahead of you, and God’s glory will enfold you.

target_units.text: Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the Lord’s glory has risen upon you.

relationship: close answer from God while the people are still speaking
rationale: Both promise God's response while the people are still speaking. Isaiah 58 gives the answer as His presence; Isaiah 65 says He listens even before their cry and asks what it is.
source_text: Then you will cry, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking He will say, “Behold, I am present.” If you remove from yourself a bond, finger-pointing, and a word of grumbling,

target_units.text: Before they cry out I will listen to them; while they are still speaking I will say, ‘What is it?’

relationship: close joining of mercy to the poor with light in darkness
rationale: Isaiah promises light in darkness after heartfelt feeding of hungry and humbled people; the psalm describes light rising in darkness for the upright and a righteous person giving to the poor. The specific act of feeding is Isaiah's formulation.
source_text: and give bread to the hungry from your heart and satisfy a humbled life, then your light will rise in darkness, and your darkness be like noon.

target_units.text: Light sprang up in darkness for the upright— merciful, compassionate and righteous.
Kind is the man who has compassion and lends; he will manage his words with judgment.
For he will never be shaken; the righteous person will be an everlasting memorial.
He will not fear an evil report; his heart is ready to hope in the Lord.
His heart is established; he shall certainly not fear, until he looks upon his enemies.
He scattered gifts; he gave to the poor. His righteousness remains for an age of an age; his horn will be raised in glory.

relationship: related unfailing growth sustained by water and divine help
rationale: Isaiah promises a drenched garden and an unfailing spring under God's continuing care; Jeremiah likens trust in the Lord to a tree beside water that does not fear a rainless year or cease bearing fruit. The garden, spring and tree are distinct images of sustained life.
source_text: Your God will be with you continually, and you will be filled as your life desires. Your bones will grow rich; you will be like a drenched garden and a spring whose water never ran out. Your bones will sprout like grass and grow rich, and they will inherit generations upon generations.

target_units.text: And blessed is the person who has trusted in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope;

and he will be like a tree flourishing beside waters, and will send its roots toward moisture, and will not fear when heat comes. Wooded stems will be upon it; in a rainless year it will not fear or cease bearing fruit.

relationship: close rebuilding of places desolated through generations
rationale: Both promise rebuilding ancient deserted places and ruined settlements associated with generations. Isaiah 58 additionally names enduring foundations and the title Builder of Fences, which Isaiah 61 does not repeat.
source_text: Your ancient deserted places will be rebuilt, and your foundations will endure through generations upon generations. You will be called Builder of Fences, and you will put an end to the paths between.

target_units.text: They will rebuild age-old deserts and raise places formerly desolated. They will renew deserted cities laid waste for generations.

relationship: legal counterpart to honoring the Sabbath by refraining from work
rationale: Isaiah calls for honoring the holy Sabbath and refraining from one's work; Deuteronomy commands keeping the Sabbath holy and doing no work, extending rest to dependents and the resident foreigner. Isaiah additionally addresses angry speech.
source_text: If you turn your foot away from the Sabbaths, from doing your wishes on the holy day, and call the Sabbaths delightful, holy to your God, you will not lift your foot for work or speak a word in anger from your mouth,

target_units.text: Keep the Sabbath day, to sanctify it, as the Lord your God commanded you.
You shall labour six days, and do all your works;

but the seventh day is a Sabbath unto the Lord your God. You shall do no work therein, you, nor your sons, nor your daughter, nor your male slave, nor your female slave, nor your ox, nor your beast of burden, nor any of your cattle, nor the sojourner dwelling with you; that your male slave and your female slave may rest as you do.

And you shall remember that you were a household slave in the land of Egypt, and that the Lord your God brought you forth thence with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm; therefore the Lord your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day, and to sanctify it.

relationship: related divine elevation and feeding from the land's abundance
rationale: Isaiah promises that God will bring the people up to earth's good things and feed Jacob's inheritance; Moses' song recounts God bringing them up upon the earth's strength and feeding field produce and other rich food. The promise and the remembered provision have different time frames.
source_text: and you will trust in the Lord. He will bring you up to earth’s good things and feed you your father Jacob’s inheritance, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken these things.’”

target_units.text: He brought them up upon the strength of the earth, and fed them the produce of the fields; they sucked honey out of the rock, and oil out of the solid rock,
butter of cattle and milk of sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, young bulls and goats, with the fat of the kernels of wheat; and they drank wine, the blood of the grape.

relationship: parallel denial that the Lord's hand lacks power
rationale: Isaiah denies that the Lord's hand cannot save; the Lord asks Moses whether His hand will not suffice to provide meat. Both reject an inference of divine inability, in different circumstances.
source_text: Is the Lord’s hand unable to save? Or has His ear grown heavy so that He cannot hear?

target_units.text: And the Lord said unto Moses: Shall the hand of the Lord not suffice? Now you shall know whether My word shall overtake you or not.

relationship: close wrongdoing causing God to turn His face away
rationale: Isaiah attributes the separation and God's turned face to the people's sins; Micah says He will turn His face away and not listen because the rulers acted wickedly. Micah's preceding accusation specifies their abuse of the people.
source_text: Instead, your offenses stand between you and God, and because of your sins He has turned His face away from you so as not to show mercy.

target_units.text: so they will cry to the Lord, but He will not listen to them. He will turn His face away from them at that time, because they acted wickedly in their practices against them.

relationship: internal bloody hands accompanying rejected prayer
rationale: Isaiah 59 names blood-defiled hands while explaining separation from God; Isaiah 1 names hands full of blood as the reason He will not listen to multiplied supplication. The surrounding settings explicitly connect misconduct and the unanswered appeal.
source_text: For your hands are stained with blood and your fingers with sins. Your lips spoke lawlessness, and your tongue meditates on injustice.

target_units.text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

relationship: related conception and birth imagery for wrongdoing
rationale: Isaiah says people conceive trouble and give birth to lawlessness; Eliphaz says the ungodly person conceives pains and his belly bears deceit. The images describe wrongdoing's production; Job's statement remains a claim within Eliphaz's speech.
source_text: No one speaks what is just, nor is there true judgment. They trust vain things and speak emptiness, for they conceive trouble and give birth to lawlessness.

target_units.text: He will conceive pains in the womb; empty things will result for him, and his belly will bear deceit.”

relationship: related useless shelter depicted through a spider's web
rationale: Isaiah says the woven web cannot become clothing or covering; Bildad says the ungodly person's tent becomes a spider's web and his house cannot endure. Clothing and housing are different inadequate protections in the two images.
source_text: Their web will not become clothing, nor will they clothe themselves from their works, for their works are works of lawlessness.

target_units.text: For his house will be uninhabited, and his tent will turn into a spider’s web.
If he props up his house, it will certainly not stand; when he takes hold of it, it will certainly not endure.

relationship: close scriptural citation of swift bloodshed and ruined ways
rationale: Romans includes swift feet pouring out blood and ruin and misery in their ways within its explicit collection of scriptural charges. These reproduce the distinctive sequence in Isaiah's indictment.
source_text: Their feet run to wickedness, quick to shed blood. Their thoughts are the thoughts of fools; destruction and misery lie in their ways.

target_units.text: Their feet are swift to pour out blood;
ruin and misery are in their ways,

relationship: close citation of not knowing the way of peace
rationale: Romans' scriptural indictment repeats that they did not know the way of peace. Isaiah additionally describes judgment's absence and twisted paths.
source_text: They do not know the way of peace, and there is no justice in their ways. For the paths they travel are twisted, and they do not know peace.

target_units.text: and the way of peace they did not know.

relationship: close expectation of light overtaken by darkness
rationale: Isaiah describes people waiting for light but encountering darkness; Jeremiah warns that people will wait for light but find death's shadow and darkness. The two passages use the same frustrated expectation in different settings.
source_text: Therefore judgment withdrew from them, and righteousness will not reach them. While they waited for light, darkness came to them; waiting for dawn, they walked in an untimely darkness.

target_units.text: Give glory to the Lord your God before darkness comes and before your feet stumble on dark mountains; you will wait for light, and there is death’s shadow, and they will be placed in darkness.

relationship: close blind groping and failure at midday
rationale: Isaiah describes groping like blind people and falling at midday as at midnight; Deuteronomy's curse describes groping at midday like a blind person in darkness. Isaiah's description supplies a concrete counterpart to the curse's imagery.
source_text: They will grope along a wall like the blind, and as though without eyes they will grope. They will fall at noon as at midnight; like people dying, they will groan.

target_units.text: And you shall grope at noonday, as the blind gropes in darkness, and He shall not prosper your ways; and you shall be wronged and plundered all your days, and there shall be none to help you.

relationship: related lament over absent judgment and rescue
rationale: Isaiah describes waiting for judgment and salvation that remain absent; Habakkuk cries to the Lord while wronged and asks why He does not listen or save. Habakkuk explicitly cries, while Isaiah's unit uses bears and traveling doves.
source_text: Like a bear and like a dove they will travel together. We waited for judgment, but there is none; salvation has withdrawn far from us.

target_units.text: How long, Lord, shall I cry and Thou wilt not listen? I shall cry to Thee while being wronged, and Thou wilt not save?

relationship: close acknowledgment of one's own sin before God
rationale: Isaiah's community acknowledges its lawless acts and sins before God; the psalmist knows his lawlessness and confesses sin against God. The shared acknowledgment is communal in Isaiah and personal in the psalm.
source_text: For our lawlessness is great before Thee, and our sins have opposed us. Our lawless deeds are within us, and we have recognized our wrongs:

target_units.text: For I know my lawlessness, and my sin is continually before me.
Against Thee alone I sinned and did evil before Thee, so that Thou mayest be justified in Thy words and prevail when Thou art judged.

relationship: parallel lying speech joined with unfaithfulness to God
rationale: Isaiah confesses lying, withdrawal from God and unrighteous words; the psalm describes lying to Him with the tongue and a heart unfaithful to His covenant. Both join deceptive speech with failed loyalty.
source_text: We acted impiously and lied and withdrew from following our God. We spoke unjust things and disobeyed; we conceived and meditated on unjust words from our heart.

target_units.text: And they deceived Him with their mouth, and lied to Him with their tongue,
but their heart was not upright with Him, nor were they faithful in His covenant.

relationship: parallel judgment prevented and distorted by wrongdoing
rationale: Isaiah's speakers say they drove judgment backward, while righteousness withdrew far away; Habakkuk says judgment is not completed and goes out distorted as the impious oppress the righteous. Their descriptions portray justice's failure through different movements.
source_text: We drove judgment backward, and righteousness has withdrawn far away, for truth was consumed in their ways, and they could not go straight through.

target_units.text: Therefore law has been scattered, and judgment is not brought to completion; the impious oppresses the righteous, so judgment will go forth distorted.

relationship: related disappearance of truth amid false speech
rationale: Isaiah says truth has been taken away; the psalm laments that truths have become few and describes deceitful speech. Isaiah additionally states God's displeasure at the absence of judgment.
source_text: Truth has been taken away, and they turned their mind away from understanding. The Lord saw, and it did not please Him that there was no judgment.

target_units.text: Save me, Lord, for the holy one is gone; for truths have become few among the sons of men.
Each spoke empty things to his neighbor; deceitful lips spoke with a heart and a heart.

relationship: close internal divine intervention when no helper is found
rationale: Both describe God looking, finding no helper and acting through His own arm. Isaiah 59 speaks of His being steadied by mercy; Isaiah 63 says His wrath stood by and His arm rescued them.
source_text: He saw, and there was no man; He considered, and there was no one to help. He defended them with His arm and steadied Himself by mercy.

target_units.text: I looked, but there was no helper; I considered, but no one came to aid. My arm rescued them, and My wrath stood by.

relationship: close adaptation of righteousness breastplate and salvation helmet
rationale: Isaiah depicts God wearing righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet; Ephesians tells believers to receive those two named pieces of armor. Isaiah's vengeance garments are not repeated in that instruction.
source_text: He put on righteousness like a breastplate, placed a helmet of salvation on His head, and wrapped Himself in a garment of vengeance and the cloak,

target_units.text: Stand, therefore, having fastened truth around your waist and put on the breastplate of righteousness,
and having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace,
in all circumstances taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.
And receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,

relationship: parallel divine armor for judgment
rationale: Both portray divine combat using righteousness as a breastplate and other moral realities as armor or weapons. Wisdom's helmet is unfeigned judgment, whereas Isaiah's is salvation; Wisdom also makes creation an ally in battle.
source_text: He put on righteousness like a breastplate, placed a helmet of salvation on His head, and wrapped Himself in a garment of vengeance and the cloak,

target_units.text: He will take His zeal as full armor and make creation into weapons to repel His enemies;
He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, and put on unfeigned judgment as a helmet;
He will take holiness as an invincible shield,
and sharpen stern wrath into a sword; the world will fight together with Him against the senseless.

relationship: parallel divine vengeance expressed as repayment
rationale: Isaiah promises recompense and repayment against adversaries; the psalm invokes the God of vengeance as earth's Judge to repay the arrogant. The psalm is a petition, while Isaiah announces the action.
source_text: as one who will repay recompense—reproach to His adversaries.

target_units.text: A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week. The God of vengeance is the Lord; the God of vengeance spoke openly.
Be exalted, Judge of the earth; give repayment to the arrogant.

relationship: close worldwide recognition of the Lord's name
rationale: Isaiah joins the west and sunrise with fear of the Lord's name and glory; Malachi says His name is glorified among nations from sunrise to sunset. Malachi adds incense and pure sacrifice; Isaiah describes anger from the Lord coming like a violent river.
source_text: Those from the west will fear the Lord’s name, and those from sunrise the glorious name. For anger from the Lord will come like a violent river; it will come with wrath.

target_units.text: “For from the sun’s rising to its setting, My name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is brought to My name, together with a pure sacrifice, because My name is great among the nations,” says the Lord Almighty.

relationship: explicit citation of the Zion deliverer turning Jacob from ungodliness
rationale: Romans introduces the deliverer's coming and the turning away of Jacob's ungodliness as written Scripture. Its coming from Zion differs from Isaiah's coming for Zion, while the Jacob clause closely corresponds.
source_text: The deliverer will come for Zion’s sake and turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

target_units.text: and in this way all Israel will be saved, just as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.

relationship: internal divine words placed and preserved in the people's mouth
rationale: Isaiah 59's covenant promises that God's Spirit and words will not fail the mouth or descendants; Isaiah 51 says God puts His words in the mouth and calls Zion His people. The enduring descendant promise belongs specifically to Isaiah 59.
source_text: “And this is My covenant with them,” said the Lord: “My spirit that is upon you and the words I put into your mouth will never fail from your mouth or your offspring’s mouth,” for the Lord said, “from now on and for ever.”

target_units.text: I will put My words in your mouth and shelter you under My hand’s shadow, by which I established heaven and founded earth; and He will say to Zion, ‘You are My people.’

relationship: covenant formula in a continuing scriptural citation
rationale: After quoting the Zion deliverer, Romans continues with God's covenant with them. Isaiah 59:21 likewise opens with that covenant formula, but develops the enduring Spirit and words; Romans instead speaks of removing sins.
source_text: “And this is My covenant with them,” said the Lord: “My spirit that is upon you and the words I put into your mouth will never fail from your mouth or your offspring’s mouth,” for the Lord said, “from now on and for ever.”

target_units.text: and in this way all Israel will be saved, just as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.
And this is My covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”

relationship: related summons to illumination from the Lord
rationale: Isaiah commands Jerusalem to be illumined because her light and the Lord's glory have come; Ephesians summons the sleeper to rise and promises Christ will shine upon him. The comparison is an illumination motif, not a claim of identical wording or addressees.
source_text: Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the Lord’s glory has risen upon you.

target_units.text: for everything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you.”

relationship: contrast between surrounding darkness and light for God's people
rationale: Isaiah places the Lord's appearing over Jerusalem against darkness covering nations; Exodus places light among Israel against Egypt's thick darkness. The historical plague and Isaiah's restoration vision have distinct settings.
source_text: Behold, darkness and gloom will cover earth over nations, but the Lord will appear upon you, and His glory will be seen over you.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a tempest throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one saw his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the sons of Israel had light everywhere they lived.

relationship: parallel light reaching nations in connection with Israel
rationale: Isaiah says nations will walk by Jerusalem's light; Simeon identifies the Child Jesus as salvation prepared for peoples, a light for the nations and glory for Israel. Luke names the Child where Isaiah addresses the illumined city.
source_text: Kings will walk by your light, and nations by your radiance.

target_units.text: because my eyes have seen Thy salvation,
which Thou didst prepare in the sight of all peoples:
a light for revelation to the nations and glory for Thy people Israel.”

relationship: close internal gathering of children carried from afar
rationale: Both describe sons being brought and daughters carried on shoulders. Isaiah 49 specifies nations and islands as the recipients of God's signal; Isaiah 60 calls the city to look at the gathering.
source_text: Lift your eyes around you and see your children gathered. Behold, all your sons have come from far away, and your daughters will be lifted upon shoulders.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “Behold, I lift My hand toward nations and will raise My signal toward islands. They will bring your sons in their bosom and carry your daughters on shoulders,

relationship: parallel nations' wealth accompanying restored glory
rationale: Isaiah describes the sea's wealth and the resources of nations coming to the city; Haggai describes the nations' choice things coming and God's house being filled with glory, naming silver and gold. The house is Haggai's immediate focus.
source_text: Then you will see and fear and be astonished in heart, for the wealth of sea, nations, and peoples will turn toward you. There will come to you

target_units.text: And I will shake all the nations, and the choice things of all the nations shall come; and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord Almighty.
The silver is Mine and the gold is Mine, says the Lord Almighty.

For the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the Lord Almighty; in this place I will give peace, says the Lord Almighty, and peace of soul as a possession for everyone building to raise this sanctuary.”

relationship: related distant visitors bringing gold and frankincense
rationale: Isaiah describes visitors from Saba bringing gold and frankincense; Matthew's eastern magi bring those gifts to the Child Jesus, with myrrh as an additional gift. Matthew does not identify them as Saba's visitors or mention Isaiah's camels.
source_text: herds of camels, and camels from Madiam and Gaipha will cover you. They will all come from Saba, bringing gold and carrying frankincense, and they will proclaim the Lord’s salvation as good news.

target_units.text: They entered the house and saw the Child with Mary His mother. Falling down, they bowed before Him; and opening their treasures, they offered Him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

relationship: parallel acceptable animal offerings in restored Zion
rationale: Isaiah describes gathered flocks accepted upon God's altar and His house glorified; the psalm asks for Jerusalem's rebuilding and anticipates delightful offerings and calves upon the altar. The named animals differ.
source_text: All Kedar’s sheep will gather to you, and Nabaioth’s rams will come to you. They will be offered acceptably upon My altar, and My house of prayer will be glorified.

target_units.text: Do good to Zion, Lord, in Thy good pleasure, and let Jerusalem’s walls be built.
Then Thou wilt delight in a sacrifice of righteousness, an offering and burnt offerings; then they will bring calves upon Thine altar.

relationship: related gifts from Tarshish and the islands
rationale: Isaiah describes waiting islands and Tharsis's ships bringing children with silver and gold; the psalm describes kings of Tarshish and islands offering gifts. The psalm's royal donors differ from Isaiah's ships carrying returning children.
source_text: Islands waited for Me, and Tharsis ships among the first, to bring your children from far away, with silver and gold, because of the Lord’s holy name and because Israel’s Holy One is glorious.

target_units.text: kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; kings of the Arabians and Saba will bring gifts.

relationship: historical counterpart to foreign royal help for Jerusalem's walls
rationale: Isaiah describes foreigners building the walls and kings attending; Nehemiah receives a foreign king's authorization for safe passage and timber for the city wall. This is a specific example of royal assistance, not an identification of every promised builder.
source_text: Foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will attend you. For because of My anger I struck you, and because of mercy I loved you.

target_units.text: I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, let him give me letters to the governors beyond the river, so that they may conduct me through until I reach Judah,

and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s park, so that he may give me timber to roof the gates, for the city wall, and for the house I will enter.” The king granted it to me, according to the good hand of God.

relationship: internal opening of city gates for people to enter
rationale: Isaiah 60 promises continually open gates for nations' resources and kings; Isaiah 26 commands opening the fortified city's gates for a people keeping righteousness and truth. Only Isaiah 60 specifies day and night openness and incoming wealth.
source_text: Your gates will be opened continually; day and night they will not be shut, to bring you the nations’ resources and kings being led.

target_units.text: Open the gates; let a people enter, keeping righteousness and keeping truth,

relationship: parallel consequences for nations refusing the restored city's order
rationale: Isaiah threatens destruction for nations and kings refusing service; Zechariah describes nations coming to Jerusalem to worship the King and a downfall upon those refusing the festival. The demanded service is specified differently.
source_text: For nations and kings who will not serve you will perish, and the nations will be utterly desolated.

target_units.text: Whoever remains from all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up each year to bow before the King, the Lord Almighty, and celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.
Whoever among all the earth’s tribes does not go up to Jerusalem to bow before the King, the Lord Almighty—these will be added to those.
If Egypt’s tribe does not go up or come there, upon these too will be the downfall with which the Lord will strike all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.
This will be Egypt’s sin and the sin of all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.

relationship: related Lebanon timber for the glory of God's house
rationale: Isaiah names Lebanon's cypress, pine and cedar for glorifying the holy place; Solomon requests Lebanon's cedar, juniper and pine for a great and glorious house. The species lists overlap without being identical.
source_text: Lebanon’s glory will come to you in cypress, pine, and cedar together, to glorify My holy place.

target_units.text: Send me cedar, juniper, and pine timbers from Lebanon, for I know your slaves know how to cut timber from Lebanon. Behold, your servants will be with my servants
and will go to prepare abundant timber for me, for the house I am building is great and glorious.

relationship: internal humbled approach to restored Zion
rationale: Isaiah 60 describes oppressors' sons coming in fear; Isaiah 49 describes kings and ruling women bowing and licking dust at the city's feet. The groups and postures differ, while the city's restored standing and recognition of the Lord connect the promises.
source_text: The sons of those who humbled and provoked you will come to you in fear. You will be called the Lord’s City, Zion of Israel’s Holy One.

target_units.text: and kings will be your foster fathers and ruling women your nurses. They will bow to you upon the earth’s surface and lick the dust of your feet. You will know that I am the Lord, and you will not be ashamed.

relationship: parallel abandonment reversed by enduring divine favor
rationale: Isaiah 60 reverses abandonment with everlasting joy; Isaiah 54 contrasts brief abandonment and anger with great, everlasting mercy. The promised reversal is shared, while joy and mercy are the particular outcomes named.
source_text: Because you became abandoned and hated, with no one helping, I will make you an everlasting exultation, joy for generations upon generations.

target_units.text: “For a short time I abandoned you, and with great mercy I will have mercy on you.
In a little anger I turned My face from you, and with everlasting mercy I will have mercy on you,” says the Lord who rescued you.

relationship: close recognition of the Lord as Israel's rescuer
rationale: Isaiah 60 names Israel's God as the One saving and delivering the city; Isaiah 49 names the Lord as rescuer and upholder of Jacob's strength. The recognition follows nations' milk and kings' wealth in the former and enemies' defeat in the latter.
source_text: You will suck the nations’ milk and eat kings’ wealth. You will know that I am the Lord who saves and delivers you, Israel’s God.

target_units.text: Those who afflicted you will eat their own flesh, drink their own blood like new wine, and become drunk. All flesh will perceive that I am the Lord who rescued you and upholds Jacob’s strength.”

relationship: internal righteous government accompanying Zion's restoration
rationale: Isaiah 60 promises rulers in peace and overseers in righteousness; Isaiah 1 restores judges and counselors and names Zion the City of Righteousness. The offices and expressions of their proper order differ.
source_text: Instead of bronze I will bring you gold, instead of iron silver, instead of wood bronze, and instead of stones iron. I will appoint your rulers in peace and your overseers in righteousness.

target_units.text: I will establish your judges as before and your counselors as at the beginning. After these things you will be called City of Righteousness, Faithful Metropolis Zion.

relationship: close salvation figured as the restored city's walls
rationale: Isaiah 60 names the walls Salvation; Isaiah 26 says salvation will become a wall and encircling wall. Isaiah 60's gates are named Engraving in this edition, not a substituted Praise.
source_text: Injustice will no longer be heard in your land, nor destruction and misery within your borders. Your walls will be called Salvation, and your gates Engraving.

target_units.text: On that day they will sing this song in Judah’s land, saying, “Behold, a fortified city! He will make our salvation a wall and an encircling wall.

relationship: parallel the Lord Himself providing light
rationale: Isaiah promises the Lord as everlasting light beyond sun and moon; Micah says the Lord will shine for the speaker sitting in darkness. Micah does not make Isaiah's claim about the heavenly lights.
source_text: The sun will not be your light by day, nor will the rising moon light your night. Instead, the Lord will be your everlasting light and God your glory.

target_units.text: Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen! I will rise, for if I sit in darkness, the Lord will shine for me.

relationship: internal end of mourning in the restored Zion setting
rationale: Isaiah 60 says the days of mourning will be fulfilled; Isaiah 35 describes those returning to Zion with everlasting gladness while pain, grief and groaning flee. Isaiah 60 additionally speaks of unsetting light.
source_text: For your sun will not set, and your moon will not fail. The Lord will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning will be fulfilled.

target_units.text: Those gathered through the Lord will return and come to Zion with gladness, everlasting gladness above their heads; for praise and exultation are upon their heads, and gladness will overtake them. Pain, grief and groaning have fled.

relationship: close righteous people inheriting land enduringly
rationale: Isaiah says all the people will be righteous and inherit the land forever; the psalm likewise says the righteous will inherit the land and dwell upon it for age upon age.
source_text: Your people will all be righteous, and they will inherit the land for ever, guarding the planting, the works of His hands, for glory.

target_units.text: But the righteous will inherit the land and dwell upon it for age upon age.

relationship: related reversal from diminished population to abundant descendants
rationale: Isaiah 60 promises that the fewest become thousands and the least a great nation; Isaiah 49 describes formerly deserted places becoming cramped with children the bereaved city did not expect. Their measures of increase differ.
source_text: The fewest will become thousands, and the least a great nation. I, the Lord, will gather them at the proper time.

target_units.text: For your deserted, destroyed, and fallen places will now be cramped by inhabitants, and those swallowing you will be removed far from you.
For your sons whom you lost will say within your hearing, ‘This place is too cramped for me. Make room for me, so I can settle.’
You will say in your heart, ‘Who bore these for me? I was childless and widowed. Who raised these for me? I was left alone; where were these of mine?’”

relationship: explicit Isaiah reading of the Spirit-anointed mission
rationale: Luke identifies the scroll as Isaiah and records Jesus reading the Spirit's anointing for good news to the poor, captives' release and the blind's sight. The wording also includes sending the oppressed away in release.
source_text: The Lord’s spirit is upon me, because He anointed me. He sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind,

target_units.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He anointed Me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed away in release,

relationship: related good news for the poor and sight for the blind in Jesus' works
rationale: Isaiah's anointed mission includes good news for the poor and sight for the blind; Jesus answers John's inquiry by naming those two works among the signs being heard and seen. Matthew's list contains other healings as well.
source_text: The Lord’s spirit is upon me, because He anointed me. He sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind,

target_units.text: Jesus answered them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see:
the blind receive sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news proclaimed to them.

relationship: explicit citation of the Lord's acceptable year
rationale: Jesus' Isaiah reading includes proclamation of the Lord's acceptable year. Luke's recorded reading stops there and does not repeat this source unit's day of recompense and comfort for mourners.
source_text: to announce the Lord’s acceptable year and a day of recompense, to comfort all who mourn,

target_units.text: to proclaim the Lord’s acceptable year.”

relationship: parallel mourning garments exchanged for gladness
rationale: Isaiah exchanges ashes and a discouraged spirit for glory, gladness and a robe of glory; the psalmist says God changed lament into dancing, tore open sackcloth and girded him with gladness. The garments and other exchanged signs differ.
source_text: so that Zion’s mourners may receive glory instead of ashes, an ointment of joy for those who mourn, a robe of glory instead of a spirit of despondency. They will be called Generations of Righteousness, the Lord’s planting, for glory.

target_units.text: Thou didst turn my lament into dancing for me; Thou didst tear open my sackcloth and gird me with gladness,

relationship: close internal rebuilding of ancient deserted places
rationale: Both describe rebuilding ancient deserted places and raising ruins associated with generations. Isaiah 61 expands the picture to deserted cities, while Isaiah 58 additionally names enduring foundations.
source_text: They will rebuild age-old deserts and raise places formerly desolated. They will renew deserted cities laid waste for generations.

target_units.text: Your ancient deserted places will be rebuilt, and your foundations will endure through generations upon generations. You will be called Builder of Fences, and you will put an end to the paths between.

relationship: internal foreign participation in the restored community's work
rationale: Isaiah 61 assigns foreigners tending flocks, plowing and vineyard work; Isaiah 60 assigns foreigners building walls and kings attending. These are different concrete forms of foreign contribution in the restoration promises.
source_text: Foreigners will come shepherding your sheep, and people of other nations will be plowmen and vinedressers.

target_units.text: Foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will attend you. For because of My anger I struck you, and because of mercy I loved you.

relationship: parallel priestly identity for God's covenant people
rationale: Isaiah promises that the people will be called priests and ministers of God; Exodus promises covenant-keeping Israel a royal priesthood and holy nation. Isaiah additionally describes receiving nations' resources.
source_text: But you will be called priests of the Lord, ministers of God. You will consume the nations’ resources and be admired in their wealth.

target_units.text: Now therefore, if you diligently listen to My voice, and keep My covenant, you shall be to Me a treasured people from among all the nations; for all the earth is Mine.
And you shall be to Me a royal priesthood and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the sons of Israel.”

relationship: parallel renewed possession of the ancestral land
rationale: Isaiah speaks of inheriting land a second time; Jeremiah promises restoration to the land God gave the fathers after gathering the dispersed. Jeremiah does not reproduce Isaiah's numerical expression or everlasting joy.
source_text: Thus they will inherit the land a second time, and everlasting joy will be over their head.

target_units.text: but, ‘The Lord lives, who brought Israel’s house up from the northern land and all the regions where they were driven.’ And I will restore them to their land that I gave their fathers.

relationship: related divine rejection of plunder
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord hates plunder arising from injustice; Malachi rejects sacrifices containing things seized by force. Malachi's offering setting is more specific than Isaiah's statement and should not be inserted into it.
source_text: “For I am the Lord who loves righteousness and hates plunder obtained through injustice. I will give their labor’s yield to righteous people and make an everlasting covenant with them.

target_units.text: “And you said, ‘These things are from hardship,’ and I blew them away,” says the Lord Almighty. “You were bringing things seized by force, the lame and the afflicted. If you bring the sacrifice, shall I accept these things from your hands?” says the Lord Almighty.

relationship: narrative counterpart to outsiders recognizing the Lord's blessing
rationale: Isaiah predicts that observers will recognize the descendants as blessed by God; Abimelech's party tells Isaac they clearly saw the Lord with him and calls him blessed by the Lord. The encounter illustrates recognition, not the whole future promise.
source_text: Their offspring and descendants will be known among nations. Everyone seeing them will recognize them, because they are offspring blessed by God,

target_units.text: And they said, “We have clearly seen that the Lord was with you, and we said, ‘Let there be an oath with a curse between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you,
“‘that you shall do us no harm, even as we have not loathed you, and as we have treated you well and sent you away in peace.’ And now you are blessed by the Lord.”

relationship: parallel clothing with salvation accompanied by rejoicing
rationale: The speaker in Isaiah rejoices in God's clothing him with a garment of salvation and tunic of joy; the psalm promises Zion's priests clothing with salvation and her holy ones exultation. Isaiah further develops bridegroom and bride adornment.
source_text: and they will rejoice greatly in the Lord.” Let my soul exult in the Lord, for He clothed me in a garment of salvation and a tunic of joy. Like a bridegroom He placed a turban on me, and like a bride He adorned me with ornaments.

target_units.text: I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will surely exult.

relationship: internal earth producing righteousness through God's action
rationale: Isaiah 61 compares God's making righteousness and exultation spring up with earth and garden growth; Isaiah 45 calls earth to bring forth mercy and righteousness together. The images place righteous flourishing within God's creative action.
source_text: As earth increases its flower and a garden its seeds, so the Lord will make righteousness and exultation spring up before all nations.

target_units.text: Let heaven above rejoice, and let clouds sprinkle righteousness. Let earth bring forth mercy and bring forth righteousness together. I am the Lord who created you.”

relationship: internal declaration that God will no longer remain silent
rationale: Isaiah 62 refuses silence for Zion's sake until her restoration appears; Isaiah 42 asks whether God will always remain silent and hold back before describing His intervention. The specific images and objects of the intervention differ.
source_text: For Zion I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem I will not let up until My righteousness goes out like light and My salvation burns like a torch.

target_units.text: “I was silent; surely I will not always be silent and hold back? I endured like a woman giving birth; I will astonish and dry up together.

relationship: internal promise of a new name from God
rationale: Isaiah 62 promises the city a new name named by the Lord; Isaiah 65 says God's servants will be called by a new name. The city and the servants are distinct immediate recipients.
source_text: Nations will see your righteousness and kings your glory. He will call you your new name, which the Lord will name.

target_units.text: For you will leave your name as a surfeit for My chosen ones, but the Lord will put you to death. Those serving Him will be called a new name,

relationship: related crown and diadem imagery associated with the Lord's hand
rationale: Isaiah calls the city a crown of beauty and royal diadem in God's hand; Wisdom says the righteous receive a splendid crown and beautiful diadem from His hand. Being the crown and receiving a crown remain distinct images.
source_text: You will be a crown of beauty in the Lord’s hand and a royal diadem in your God’s hand.

target_units.text: Therefore they will receive the royal crown of splendor and the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand, because with His right hand He will cover them and with His arm He will shield them.

relationship: parallel changed names expressing renewed divine belonging
rationale: Isaiah replaces Abandoned and Desert with My Desire and Inhabited; Hosea reverses Not Shown Mercy and Not My People through mercy and belonging. The names differ while each reversal expresses restored relationship with God.
source_text: You will no longer be called Abandoned, nor will your land be called Desert. You will be called My Desire, and your land Inhabited.

target_units.text: I will sow her for Myself upon the land, show mercy to Not Shown Mercy and say to Not My People, ‘You are My people.’ He will say, ‘Thou art the Lord my God!’”

relationship: close divine rejoicing over restored Zion
rationale: Isaiah likens God's rejoicing over the city to a bridegroom's delight in his bride; Zephaniah says the Lord will renew her in love and rejoice over her with delight. Zephaniah's comparison is a feast day rather than marriage.
source_text: As a young man lives with a virgin, so your sons will dwell with you. As a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so the Lord will rejoice over you.

target_units.text: The Lord your God is within you; mighty, He shall save you. He shall bring gladness upon you, and renew you in His love; and He shall rejoice over you with delight, as on a day of feasting.”

relationship: related day-and-night remembrance and appeal to God
rationale: Isaiah's appointed guards are never silent day or night as they remember the Lord; Luke describes God's chosen ones crying to Him day and night for justice. Luke's surrounding parable explicitly teaches persistent prayer.
source_text: Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I appointed guards all day and all night, who will never be silent as they remember the Lord.

target_units.text: And will not God bring about justice for His chosen ones who cry to Him day and night? And will He delay over them?

relationship: related restoration making the community renowned throughout earth
rationale: Isaiah's conditional clause speaks of God restoring Jerusalem and making her a source of pride on earth; Zephaniah promises restored people renown and a boast among earth's peoples. This does not substitute a command to give God no rest for Isaiah's native wording.
source_text: For there is no one like you, if He restores Jerusalem and makes her a source of pride upon earth.

target_units.text: Look, I am acting within you for your sake at that time, says the Lord. I will save the oppressed and the rejected; I will receive them and make them a boast and renowned throughout the earth.

They will be ashamed at that time, when I do good to you and when I receive you. I will make you renowned and a boast among all the earth’s peoples, when I turn your captivity before you, says the Lord.

relationship: reversal of the curse of foreigners consuming the land's produce
rationale: Isaiah promises that enemies and foreigners will no longer consume the people's grain and wine; Deuteronomy's curse says an unknown nation will consume the land's yield and their labors. The reversal concerns who enjoys the produce.
source_text: The Lord swore by His right hand and the strength of His arm: “I will no longer give your grain and food to your enemies, nor will foreigners drink your wine for which you toiled.

target_units.text: A nation which you do not know shall consume the yield of your land and all your labours; and you shall be wronged and crushed all your days.

relationship: parallel enjoying the produce of one's own labor
rationale: Isaiah promises that those gathering will eat and drink their produce; the psalm promises eating the labors of one's own hands. Isaiah additionally names praise and drinking in God's holy dwellings.
source_text: Instead, those who gather will eat these things and praise the Lord, and those who gather will drink them in My holy dwellings.”

target_units.text: You will eat the labors of your wrists; happy are you, and it will be well with you.

relationship: internal preparation of a cleared road
