rationale: Isaiah 62 commands road preparation and scattering stones; Isaiah 40 commands preparing the Lord's way and describes crooked and rough places becoming straight and level. The specified obstacles differ.
source_text: Go through My gates and make a road for My people. Scatter the stones from the road; raise a signal for the nations!

target_units.text: A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.
Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low; all the crooked places will become straight, and the rough country will become plains.

relationship: close announcement to daughter Zion of a saving arrival
rationale: Isaiah tells daughter Zion that her Savior comes; Zechariah tells daughter Zion her king comes, righteous and saving. Zechariah specifies the king's gentleness and mount, which Isaiah does not name here.
source_text: For behold, the Lord has made it heard to earth’s farthest end: “Tell daughter Zion, ‘Behold, the savior is arriving for you, bringing His own reward and His work before His face.’”

target_units.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; proclaim, daughter Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saving, gentle, and mounted upon a beast of burden and a young colt.

relationship: close internal coming with reward and work before Him
rationale: Both announce an arrival with reward and work before the coming figure. Isaiah 62 tells daughter Zion that the savior is arriving; Isaiah 40 names the Lord and emphasizes might and dominion.
source_text: For behold, the Lord has made it heard to earth’s farthest end: “Tell daughter Zion, ‘Behold, the savior is arriving for you, bringing His own reward and His work before His face.’”

target_units.text: Behold, the Lord comes with might, and His arm with dominion; behold, His reward is with Him, and His work before Him.

relationship: parallel people named holy and redeemed by the Lord
rationale: Isaiah names the restored community Holy People and Redeemed by the Lord; Deuteronomy identifies Israel as the Lord's holy people and recalls redemption from Egypt's bondage. Isaiah's new city titles are additional.
source_text: He will call it a holy people redeemed by the Lord; but you will be called a sought-out city, not abandoned.

target_units.text: For you are a holy people unto the Lord your God; and the Lord your God has chosen you to be unto Him a people for His own possession, above all the nations upon the face of the earth.
The Lord preferred you and chose you, not because you were more numerous than all the nations, for you are the fewest of all the nations,

but because the Lord loved you, and kept the oath which He sware unto your fathers, the Lord brought you forth with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, out of the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

relationship: close internal judgment associated with Edom and Bosor
rationale: Isaiah 63 introduces the red-robed arrival from Edom and Bosor; Isaiah 34 locates the Lord's bloody sacrifice and slaughter in Idumea and Bosor. The named territory and city tie the scenes together without making their images identical.
source_text: Who is this arriving from Edom, with redness of garments from Bosor, so beautiful in His robe, with force and strength? “I speak righteousness and saving judgment.”

target_units.text: My sword became drunk in heaven. Behold, it will descend upon Idumea and upon the people of destruction, with judgment.
The Lord’s sword was filled with blood, thickened with lambs’ fat and the fat of male goats and rams, for the Lord has a sacrifice in Bosor and a great slaughter in Idumea.

relationship: literal same-chapter question and answer about red garments
rationale: The question compares the red clothing to a trodden winepress; the following answer describes trampling the nations in wrath and bringing their blood to earth. This immediate literary explanation connects the stained garments with judgment.
source_text: Why are Thy garments red and Thy clothes as though from a trodden winepress?

target_units.text: “I am full of what has been trodden. No man from the nations is with Me. I trampled them in wrath, crushed them like earth, and brought their blood down to earth.

relationship: parallel treading imagery for judgment upon nations
rationale: Isaiah's answer about winepress-like garments describes trampling nations in wrath; Joel's judgment of nations calls for treading a full winepress because their evils multiplied. The actors and wording of the treading differ.
source_text: “I am full of what has been trodden. No man from the nations is with Me. I trampled them in wrath, crushed them like earth, and brought their blood down to earth.

target_units.text: Let all the nations be roused and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, because there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
Send out sickles, because the vintage is at hand! Enter and tread, because the winepress is full; the vats overflow, because their evils have multiplied.

relationship: close paired day and year of divine recompense
rationale: Isaiah 63 pairs a day of recompense with a year of redemption; Isaiah 34 pairs the Lord's day of judgment with a year of repayment for Zion's judgment. Redemption and repayment are distinct descriptions of the year.
source_text: For a day of recompense came upon them, and a year of redemption is here.

target_units.text: For it is the Lord’s day of judgment and a year of repayment for Zion’s judgment.

relationship: close divine action through His own arm when no helper is found
rationale: Both describe the absence of a helper followed by God's own arm acting. Isaiah 63 says the arm rescued them and wrath stood by; Isaiah 59 speaks of His being steadied by mercy.
source_text: I looked, but there was no helper; I considered, but no one came to aid. My arm rescued them, and My wrath stood by.

target_units.text: He saw, and there was no man; He considered, and there was no one to help. He defended them with His arm and steadied Himself by mercy.

relationship: internal judgment leaving blood upon the earth
rationale: Isaiah 63 says God trampled in anger and brought the victims' blood to earth; Isaiah 34 says the earth becomes drunk with blood in the Idumean judgment. The descriptions share the bloodied earth while using different images.
source_text: I trampled them in My anger and brought their blood down to earth.”

target_units.text: The stout ones will fall with them, and rams and bulls; the earth will become drunk with blood and be filled with their fat.

relationship: close remembrance of God's repayments and mercy
rationale: Isaiah remembers the Lord's mercy and excellent deeds in what He repays; the psalm commands remembering His repayments and names redemption, mercy and compassion. The psalm's imperative and Isaiah's recollection serve the same thankful remembrance.
source_text: I remembered the Lord’s mercy, the Lord’s excellent deeds in everything He repays us. The Lord is a good judge for Israel’s house; He brings upon us according to His mercy and the abundance of His righteousness.

target_units.text: Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all His repayments:
who is gracious toward all your lawless deeds, who heals all your diseases;
who redeems your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassions;

relationship: parallel Israel described as God's children in a rescue setting
rationale: Isaiah calls the people God's children and describes His becoming their salvation; Exodus calls Israel His firstborn son while demanding release from Pharaoh. Collective sonship accompanies God's action for the people in both.
source_text: He said, “Are they not My people, children who will surely not reject Me?” And He became their salvation

target_units.text: And you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is My firstborn son.
And I said to you, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” If therefore you will not let them go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.’”

relationship: close God's own rescue motivated by love
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord Himself saved and redeemed them because He loved them; Deuteronomy says He loved the fathers, chose their offspring and Himself brought them from Egypt. Isaiah expressly contrasts the Lord Himself with an envoy or angel.
source_text: from every affliction. Neither an envoy nor an angel, but the Lord Himself saved them because He loved and spared them. He Himself redeemed them, took them up, and exalted them throughout all the days of the age.

target_units.text: Because He loved your fathers, He chose their seed after them, even you, and Himself brought you forth out of Egypt by His great strength,

relationship: related warning against offending God's Holy Spirit
rationale: Isaiah recounts disobedience that provoked God's holy spirit and brought hostility; Ephesians commands believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit in whom they were sealed for redemption. The narrated consequence and the exhortation differ.
source_text: But they disobeyed and provoked His holy spirit. He turned toward hostility against them and Himself fought them.

target_units.text: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

relationship: related bringing up of the sheep's shepherd
rationale: Isaiah speaks of bringing the sheep's shepherd up from earth; Hebrews names God bringing the great shepherd of the sheep, Jesus, up from the dead. The shared shepherd and bringing-up language does not turn Isaiah's earth into an explicit statement of resurrection.
source_text: The one who brought the sheep’s shepherd up from earth remembered days of old. Where is the one who placed the holy spirit among them,

target_units.text: Now may the God of peace, who brought up from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus, in the blood of an eternal covenant,

relationship: historical counterpart to Moses and divine mastery of water
rationale: Isaiah recalls God leading Moses and overpowering water; Exodus narrates Moses extending his hand, the Lord driving back the sea and Israel crossing on dry ground. Isaiah condenses the event into divine guidance and glory.
source_text: who led Moses by the right hand, the arm of His glory? He overpowered water before Him to make Himself an everlasting name.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: close guidance through the deep compared with a wilderness
rationale: Isaiah describes leading them through the abyss like a horse through a wilderness; the psalm says God guided them through the deep as in a wilderness. Isaiah adds that they did not grow weary.
source_text: He led them through the abyss like a horse through a wilderness, and they did not grow weary.

target_units.text: He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up; He guided them in the deep as in a wilderness.

relationship: close the Lord's Spirit guiding on level terrain
rationale: Isaiah compares the Spirit's guidance to livestock passing through a plain; the psalm declares that God's good Spirit will lead the speaker on level ground. The collective remembrance and personal declaration share the guiding Spirit and terrain image.
source_text: Like livestock through a plain, a spirit from the Lord came down and guided them. So Thou didst lead Thy people to make Thyself a glorious name.

target_units.text: Teach me to do Thy will, for Thou art my God. Thy good Spirit will lead me on level ground.

relationship: close appeal for God to look from His holy heavenly house
rationale: Isaiah asks God to turn and see from His holy, glorious house in heaven; Deuteronomy asks Him to look from His holy house in heaven and bless Israel. Isaiah's appeal particularly questions withheld compassion.
source_text: Turn from heaven and see from Thy holy and glorious house. Where are Thy zeal and strength? Where is the abundance of Thy mercy and compassion, since Thou hast held back from us?

target_units.text: Look down from Thy holy house, from heaven, and bless Thy people Israel, and the land which Thou hast given them, as Thou didst swear unto our fathers to give us a land flowing with milk and honey.

relationship: parallel confession of the Lord as Israel's Father
rationale: Isaiah twice calls the Lord our Father despite unrecognition by Abraham and Israel; Moses' song calls Him the people's Father who acquired, made and created them. Only Isaiah contrasts Him with named human ancestors.
source_text: For Thou art our Father, because Abraham did not know us and Israel did not recognize us. But Thou, Lord, art our Father. Rescue us! From the beginning Thy name has been upon us.

target_units.text: Do you thus repay the Lord, O foolish people and unwise? Is not He Himself your Father, who acquired you, and made you, and created you?

relationship: related attribution of hardening to God
rationale: Isaiah's communal question attributes straying and hardened hearts to God; Romans states that He hardens whom He wills. The lament's request that He return and Romans' argument about mercy retain their distinct settings.
source_text: Why, Lord, didst Thou make us stray from Thy way and harden our hearts so that we do not fear Thee? Return because of Thy servants, because of the tribes of Thine inheritance,

target_units.text: So then, He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens.

relationship: close lament over adversaries violating God's sanctuary
rationale: Isaiah says adversaries trampled God's sanctuary; the psalm says nations entered His inheritance and defiled His holy temple. Both lament violated sacred space without naming identical attackers here.
source_text: so that we may inherit a little of Thy holy mountain. Our adversaries trampled Thy sanctuary.

target_units.text: A psalm for Asaph. God, nations entered Thine inheritance; they defiled Thy holy temple; they made Jerusalem into a fruit-watchman’s hut.

relationship: parallel divine manifestation shaking mountains
rationale: Isaiah imagines heaven opened and mountains trembling and melting before God; Micah describes the Lord descending, mountains shaken and valleys melting. The particular terrain that melts differs.
source_text: We became as at the beginning, when Thou didst not rule us and Thy name had not been called upon us. If Thou openest heaven, trembling will seize mountains because of Thee, and they will melt,

target_units.text: For look, the Lord is coming out of His place; He will descend and step upon the heights of the earth,
and the mountains will be shaken beneath Him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire and like water flowing downhill.

relationship: close wax melting before fire as an image of judgment
rationale: Isaiah compares melting to wax before fire and says adversaries will burn; the psalm asks that sinners perish before God as wax melts before fire. The psalm is a petition, while Isaiah describes the expected manifestation.
source_text: like wax melting before fire. Fire will burn up the adversaries, and the Lord’s name will become manifest among the adversaries. Nations will be shaken before Thee.

target_units.text: As smoke vanishes, let them vanish; as wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before God.

relationship: parallel mountains responding to God's manifestation
rationale: Isaiah says glorious divine acts bring trembling upon mountains; Habakkuk describes God standing and looking, followed by the earth shaking and mountains being violently crushed. Their precise descriptions of the mountains' response differ.
source_text: Whenever Thou dost glorious things, trembling will seize mountains because of Thee.

target_units.text: He stood, and the earth shook; He looked, and nations melted. Mountains were crushed violently; everlasting hills melted.

relationship: related unseen and unheard divine works in Paul's scriptural citation
rationale: Isaiah speaks of not hearing or seeing a god except the Lord and His works for those awaiting mercy; Paul's citation speaks of unseen and unheard things prepared for those loving God. The eye-and-ear pattern corresponds, but the objects and beneficiaries are not worded identically.
source_text: From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a god except Thee and Thy works, which Thou wilt do for those awaiting mercy.

target_units.text: But as it is written, “What an eye has not seen and an ear has not heard, and what has not arisen in a human heart—these are the things God prepared for those who love Him.”

relationship: related polluted clothing imagery for lawlessness
rationale: Isaiah calls the people's righteousness a menstruating woman's rag; Zechariah portrays Joshua in filthy garments whose removal is explained as removal of lawless deeds. The corporate comparison and the priest's symbolic clothing remain distinct.
source_text: We all became like unclean people; all our righteousness is like a menstruating woman’s rag. We fell away like leaves because of our lawless deeds; thus wind will carry us off.

target_units.text: Joshua was clothed in filthy garments and standing before the angel.
He answered and said to those standing before him, “Remove the filthy garments from him.” He said to him, “Look, I have taken away your lawless deeds; clothe him in a robe reaching to the feet,

relationship: parallel absence of people seeking God
rationale: Isaiah laments no one calling God's name or remembering to hold to Him; the psalm describes God looking for anyone seeking Him, followed by all turning aside. Isaiah additionally describes God's turned face and His handing the people over because of sins.
source_text: There is no one calling on Thy name or remembering to take hold of Thee, because Thou didst turn Thy face away from us and didst hand us over because of our sins.

target_units.text: The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.

All turned aside; together they became useless; there is no one who shows kindness, not even one. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they practiced deceit. The venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood; brokenness and misery are in their ways, and they did not know a way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes.

relationship: close people as clay in God's hands
rationale: Isaiah calls the people clay and the work of God's hands; Jeremiah explicitly likens Israel to a potter's clay in His hands. The potter is named in Jeremiah, while Isaiah also names God as Father.
source_text: But now, Lord, Thou art our Father, and we are clay, all the work of Thy hands.

target_units.text: Can I not shape you as this potter does, house of Israel? Behold, you are like the potter’s clay in My hands.

relationship: close request that God not remember the people's sins
rationale: Isaiah asks God not to remember sins at the appointed time; the psalm asks Him not to remember ancient lawless acts and to bring compassion quickly. Their temporal expressions differ.
source_text: Do not be exceedingly angry with us or remember our sins at the appointed time. And now look, for we are all Thy people.

target_units.text: Do not remember our ancient acts of lawlessness; let Thy compassions swiftly reach us first, for we became very poor.

relationship: parallel lament over deserted Zion and Jerusalem
rationale: Isaiah describes the holy city and Zion as desert and Jerusalem as a curse; Lamentations describes Jerusalem left alone and Zion's roads empty of festival visitors. The deserted city is shared, while the details of its desolation differ.
source_text: The city of Thy holy place became a desert; Zion became like a desert, Jerusalem a curse.

target_units.text: After Israel was taken captive and Jerusalem laid waste, Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lament over Jerusalem, saying: How the city once full of peoples sat alone! She has become like a widow, she who was populous among the nations. A ruler among the regions has become subject to tribute.
Weeping, she wept in the night, her tears upon her cheeks. Among all those who love her there is no one to comfort her. All her friends have dealt faithlessly with her; they have become her enemies.
Judea was deported because of her humiliation and her great slavery. She dwelt among the nations; she found no rest. All her pursuers overtook her among those who afflicted her.
Zion’s roads mourn because no one comes at the festival. All her gates are destroyed; her priests groan. Her virgins are led away, and she is embittered within herself.

relationship: historical account of the burning of the Lord's house
rationale: Isaiah laments the holy house becoming fire-burned; Kings narrates the chief cook setting fire to the Lord's house and Jerusalem's houses. The historical narrative supplies a concrete temple-burning counterpart to the lament.
source_text: The house, our holy place, and the glory our ancestors blessed became fire-burned, and all the glorious things collapsed.

target_units.text: He set fire to the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all Jerusalem’s houses; every house was set ablaze by
the chief cook.

relationship: related complaint that God withholds action after sanctuary destruction
rationale: Isaiah says God held back and remained silent despite the preceding devastation; the psalm, after lamenting the burnt sanctuary, asks why He turns His hand away. The complaints use silence and a withdrawn hand respectively.
source_text: Despite all these things Thou didst hold back, Lord, and keep silent and humble us greatly.

target_units.text: How long, God, will the enemy reproach? Will the adversary provoke Thy name to the end?
Why dost Thou turn away Thy hand and Thy right hand from within Thy bosom to the end?

relationship: explicit Isaiah citation of God found by those not seeking Him
rationale: Romans names Isaiah and repeats God's being found and made known among people who did not seek or ask for Him. Isaiah's additional announcement to a nation not calling His name is not included in that verse's quotation.
source_text: “I became manifest to those not seeking Me; I was found by those not inquiring of Me. I said, ‘Here I am,’ to the nation that did not call My name.

target_units.text: And Isaiah speaks boldly and says, “I was found among those who did not seek Me; I became known to those who did not ask for Me.”

relationship: explicit citation of extended hands toward a disobedient people
rationale: Romans quotes the all-day stretching out of God's hands toward a disobedient, contrary people and identifies the subject as Israel. Isaiah further describes their untrue path and following sins.
source_text: I spread out My hands all day to a disobedient, contradicting people who did not walk in a true way but followed their sins.

target_units.text: But concerning Israel He says, “All day long I stretched out My hands toward a disobedient and contrary people.”

relationship: parallel condemnation of sacrifices to demons rather than God
rationale: Isaiah condemns sacrifices and incense to demons that do not exist; Deuteronomy says the people sacrificed to demons and not God. Deuteronomy does not repeat Isaiah's explicit statement that these demons do not exist.
source_text: This people continually provokes Me to My face. They sacrifice in gardens and burn incense on bricks to demons that do not exist,

target_units.text: They sacrificed unto demons, and not unto God, unto gods whom they did not know; new ones, lately come, whom their fathers did not know.

relationship: legal counterpart to the accusation of eating pig's flesh
rationale: Isaiah includes pig's flesh among defiled practices; Leviticus calls the pig unclean and forbids eating its flesh. Isaiah's tombs, caves and sacrificial broth are additional accusations.
source_text: and sleep in tombs and caves for dreams. They eat pig’s flesh and sacrificial broth; all their vessels are defiled.

target_units.text: and the pig, because it divides the hoof and has cleft hoof-claws but does not bring up the cud; it is unclean for you.
You shall not eat their flesh or touch their carcasses; they are unclean for you.

relationship: related rejection of self-exalting religious separation
rationale: Isaiah's speakers tell others to keep away because they are clean; Luke's parable targets people trusting their own righteousness and despising others, illustrated by the Pharisee's contrast with other people. The claimed cleanliness and claimed righteousness are distinct forms of self-exaltation.
source_text: They say, ‘Far away from me! Do not approach me, for I am clean.’ This is smoke of My wrath; fire burns in it all the days.

target_units.text: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded the rest as nothing:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed these things to himself: ‘God, I thank Thee that I am not like the rest of humanity—plunderers, unrighteous people, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week; I tithe everything I acquire.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner.’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

relationship: close recompense into the offender's lap or bosom
rationale: Isaiah announces God will repay into their lap; the psalm petitions Him to repay neighbors' insults into their bosom. The repayment image corresponds, while the psalm additionally specifies sevenfold recompense.
source_text: Behold, it is written before Me: I will not keep silent until I repay into their lap

target_units.text: Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom their insult with which they insulted Thee, Lord.

relationship: related reckoning with ancestral sins and later generations
rationale: Isaiah names the people's sins together with their ancestors' sins; Exodus describes repayment of fathers' sins upon children of those hating God. Isaiah explicitly includes the present people's own deeds rather than attributing the whole charge only to ancestors.
source_text: their sins and their ancestors’ sins,” says the Lord, “who burned incense on mountains and insulted Me on hills. I will repay their works into their lap.”

target_units.text: You shall not bow down to them, neither shall you serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Me,

relationship: parallel sparing a larger group for the righteous within it
rationale: Isaiah's preserved grape illustrates not destroying everyone for the sake of the Lord's servant; God tells Abraham He would spare Sodom if fifty righteous people were found within it. The conditional promise is the parallel, not a claim that Sodom was ultimately spared.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “As a grape is found in the cluster and people say, ‘Do not ruin it, for the Lord’s blessing is in it,’ so I will act for the sake of the one serving Me; for this one’s sake I will not destroy everyone.

target_units.text: And the Lord said, “If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake.”

relationship: close descendants of God's servants inheriting restored Zion
rationale: Isaiah promises Jacob's and Judah's offspring inheritance of the holy mountain; the psalm promises salvation for Zion and rebuilt Judean cities possessed by His servants' offspring. Both join restoration, descendants and inherited dwelling.
source_text: I will bring out the offspring from Jacob and from Judah, and it will inherit My holy mountain. My chosen ones and My slaves will inherit and dwell there.

target_units.text: For God will save Zion, and Judea’s cities will be built; they will dwell there and inherit it.
His servants’ offspring will possess it, and those loving His name will dwell in it.

relationship: contrast between Achor's judgment memory and promised pastoral rest
rationale: Joshua recounts Achar's judgment in Achor and the place's enduring name; Isaiah promises that ravine as a resting place for cattle belonging to the people seeking God. The same named place moves from a judgment narrative to a promised use for the restored people.
source_text: There will be shelters for flocks in the woodland, and the ravine of Achor will be a resting place for cattle, for My people who sought Me.

target_units.text: Joshua took Achar son of Zerah and brought him up to the ravine of Achor, with his sons, his daughters, his cattle, his beasts of burden, all his sheep, his tent, and everything belonging to him. All the people were with him, and he brought them up to Emek-achor.
Joshua said to Achar, “Why have you brought destruction upon us? May the Lord destroy you, as on this very day!” And all Israel stoned him with stones.
They set a great heap of stones over him. The Lord ceased from the heat of His anger. Therefore the place was named Emek-achor, as it is to this day.

relationship: close rejection of a table and drink associated with demons
rationale: Isaiah condemns a table for the demon and mixed drink for Fortune; Paul excludes participation in demons' table and cup alongside the Lord's. Fortune is separately named only in Isaiah.
source_text: But you who abandoned Me and forget My holy mountain, preparing a table for the demon and filling a mixed drink for Fortune,

target_units.text: Rather, that what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. And I do not want you to become participants with demons.
You cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons.

relationship: parallel rejected calling followed by calamity
rationale: Isaiah's Lord says He called without obedience and will hand the people to the sword; personified Wisdom says she called without obedience and describes coming destruction and an unanswered return call. The speakers and particular judgments differ.
source_text: I will hand you over to the sword; all of you will fall in slaughter, because I called you and you did not obey, I spoke and you disregarded Me. You did evil before Me and chose what I did not want.”

target_units.text: Since I kept calling and you did not obey, and kept extending words and you paid no attention,
but you were making my counsels ineffective and disobeyed my reproofs,
therefore I too will laugh at your ruin and exult when destruction comes to you,
and when sudden tumult reaches you and overthrow arrives like a storm, when affliction and siege come upon you, or when destruction comes to you.
For when you call upon me, I will not listen to you; evil people will seek me and will not find me,

relationship: related opposed outcomes of hunger and satisfaction
rationale: Isaiah contrasts God's servants eating and drinking with rebels' hunger and thirst; Luke blesses the presently hungry with future filling and warns the presently filled of hunger. Luke's present and future reversal is not identical to Isaiah's division of the two groups.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: “Behold, those serving Me will eat, but you will hunger. Those serving Me will drink, but you will thirst. Those serving Me will rejoice, but you will be ashamed.

target_units.text: Lifting His eyes toward His disciples, He said, “Blessed are you who are poor, because yours is God’s kingdom.
Blessed are you who hunger now, because you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, because you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, when they exclude you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man.
Rejoice on that day and leap, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; their fathers treated the prophets in the same way.
But woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation.
Woe to you who are filled now, because you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, because you will mourn and weep.

relationship: related contrasting outcomes of joy and mourning
rationale: Isaiah contrasts servants' joy with others' heartache and wailing; Luke contrasts future laughter for those weeping now with mourning for those laughing now. The temporal reversal in Luke differs from Isaiah's stated separation of servants and opponents.
source_text: Behold, those serving Me will exult with joy, but you will cry out because of your heart’s pain and wail from a broken spirit.

target_units.text: Blessed are you who hunger now, because you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, because you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, when they exclude you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man.
Rejoice on that day and leap, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; their fathers treated the prophets in the same way.
But woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation.
Woe to you who are filled now, because you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, because you will mourn and weep.

relationship: internal promise that God gives a new name
rationale: Isaiah 65 promises a new name for God's servants; Isaiah 62 promises the city a new name from the Lord. This connection concerns the new-name clause, not an alteration of Isaiah 65's native word surfeit.
source_text: For you will leave your name as a surfeit for My chosen ones, but the Lord will put you to death. Those serving Him will be called a new name,

target_units.text: Nations will see your righteousness and kings your glory. He will call you your new name, which the Lord will name.

relationship: related truthful swearing and blessing in relation to the Lord
rationale: Isaiah joins blessing the true God with swearing by Him; Jeremiah joins swearing that the Lord lives in truth and righteousness with nations' blessing and praise of God in Jerusalem. Jeremiah's pronouns and phrasing of the blessing are not identical.
source_text: which will be blessed upon earth. For they will bless the true God, and those swearing upon earth will swear by the true God. They will forget their former affliction, and it will not rise into their heart.

target_units.text: and swears, ‘The Lord lives,’ with truth and in judgment and righteousness, then nations will bless in her, and in Him they will praise God in Jerusalem.

relationship: close expectation of new heavens and a new earth
rationale: Isaiah promises new heaven and earth; Second Peter says believers await new heavens and earth according to God's promise and specifies righteousness dwelling there. Isaiah adds forgetting former things.
source_text: For heaven will be new and earth new, and they will never remember former things, nor will those things enter their heart,

target_units.text: But according to His promise we await new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

relationship: parallel Jerusalem and God's people restored to joy
rationale: Isaiah says God makes Jerusalem exultation and His people joy; Zephaniah summons daughter Jerusalem to rejoice and describes God's saving presence and delight over her. The divine and communal rejoicing are intertwined in both settings.
source_text: but they will find joy and exultation in it. For behold, I am making Jerusalem an exultation and My people joy.

target_units.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion! Proclaim, daughter Jerusalem! Be glad and delight with all your heart, daughter Jerusalem!
The Lord removed your wrongdoings and has redeemed you from your enemies’ hand. The Lord, King of Israel, is within you; you will see evils no more.
At that time the Lord will say to Jerusalem, “Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands hang loose.
The Lord your God is within you; mighty, He shall save you. He shall bring gladness upon you, and renew you in His love; and He shall rejoice over you with delight, as on a day of feasting.”

relationship: internal removal of weeping in God's saving work
rationale: Isaiah 65 promises that weeping and crying will no longer be heard in Jerusalem; Isaiah 25 says God removed every tear from every face. The local city promise and the broader expression retain their different scopes.
source_text: I will exult over Jerusalem and rejoice over My people, and no sound of weeping or crying will ever again be heard in her.

target_units.text: Death swallowed, having prevailed; and again God removed every tear from every face. He removed the people’s reproach from all the earth, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken.

relationship: reversal of the curse of building and planting without enjoyment
rationale: Isaiah promises building houses for one's own habitation and planting vineyards for one's own food; Deuteronomy threatens building without dwelling and planting without harvesting. The corresponding acts receive opposite outcomes.
source_text: They will build houses and inhabit them themselves; they will plant vineyards and eat their own produce.

target_units.text: You shall take a wife, and another man shall have her; you shall build a house, and shall not dwell therein; you shall plant a vineyard, and shall not gather its fruit.

relationship: parallel enduring enjoyment of restored homes and crops
rationale: Isaiah promises that others will not inhabit the builders' houses or eat the planters' produce; Amos promises restored cities inhabited by the people and vineyards and gardens whose produce they enjoy, without renewed uprooting. Isaiah's tree-of-life comparison is additional.
source_text: They will not build for others to inhabit or plant for others to eat. For My people’s days will be like those of the tree of life; they will wear out the works of their labor.

target_units.text: I will reverse the captivity of My people Israel. They will build ruined cities and inhabit them, plant vineyards and drink their wine, plant gardens and eat their fruit.
I will plant them upon their land, and they will certainly never again be uprooted from the land I have given them,” says the Lord God Almighty.

relationship: contrast between blessed descendants remaining and children lost to captivity
rationale: Isaiah promises children not born for a curse and descendants remaining with God's blessed offspring; Deuteronomy's curse describes children who will not belong to their parents because of captivity. The comparison concerns family continuity rather than an identical description of childbirth.
source_text: My chosen ones will not labor in vain or bear children for a curse, because they are offspring blessed by God, and their descendants will be with them.

target_units.text: You shall beget sons and daughters, but they shall not be yours; for they shall go into captivity.

relationship: close internal answer while the people are still speaking
rationale: Both promise God's answer while the people are still speaking. Isaiah 65 also says He listens before their cry; Isaiah 58 expresses His answer as His presence.
source_text: Before they cry out I will listen to them; while they are still speaking I will say, ‘What is it?’

target_units.text: Then you will cry, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking He will say, “Behold, I am present.” If you remove from yourself a bond, finger-pointing, and a word of grumbling,

relationship: close internal peaceful animals on God's holy mountain
rationale: Both describe wolves with lambs, lions eating straw with oxen and no destructive harm on God's holy mountain. Isaiah 65 adds the serpent eating earth like bread, which the earlier animal scene does not say.
source_text: Then wolves and lambs will graze together, and a lion will eat straw like an ox, while a serpent will eat earth like bread. They will not wrong or destroy on My holy mountain,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: And the wolf will feed with the lamb, and the leopard will rest with the young goat; and the calf and the bull and the lion will feed together, and a little child will lead them.
And the ox and the bear will feed together, and their young will be together; and the lion and the ox will eat straw together.
And an infant will stretch out his hand over the hole of asps, and over the nest of their young.

And they will certainly do no harm, nor will they be able at all to destroy anyone upon My holy mountain; for the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.

relationship: close serpent eating earth
rationale: Isaiah's peaceful-animal scene retains the serpent eating earth like bread; Genesis' sentence upon the serpent includes eating earth throughout its life. The shared food does not erase the different settings of curse and future peace.
source_text: Then wolves and lambs will graze together, and a lion will eat straw like an ox, while a serpent will eat earth like bread. They will not wrong or destroy on My holy mountain,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: And the Lord God said to the serpent: Because you have done this, cursed are you above all cattle and all the wild beasts of the earth. Upon your breast and belly you shall go, and earth you shall eat all the days of your life.

relationship: explicit prophetic citation of heaven as throne and earth as footstool
rationale: Acts introduces the prophet's saying and repeats heaven as God's throne, earth as His footstool and the questions about a house and place of rest. The surrounding speech contrasts this with a house made by human hands.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “Heaven is My throne, and earth the footstool of My feet. What sort of house will you build for Me, or what place is My rest?

target_units.text: ‘Heaven is My throne, and the earth the footstool of My feet. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or what place is there for My rest?

relationship: close throne and footstool language applied to oaths
rationale: Matthew's instruction against swearing by heaven or earth names them God's throne and His feet's footstool. Isaiah uses those same images in a question about building God's house, not directly about oaths.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “Heaven is My throne, and earth the footstool of My feet. What sort of house will you build for Me, or what place is My rest?

target_units.text: But I tell you: do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God,
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of His feet, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.

relationship: close continuation of the citation concerning God's creating hand
rationale: Acts continues the prophetic citation by asking whether God's hand made all these things; Isaiah asserts that His hand made them and that they are His. Acts does not repeat this unit's following description of the humble hearer.
source_text: For My hand made all these things, and all these things are Mine,” says the Lord. “And to whom will I look except the humble and quiet one who trembles at My words?

target_units.text: Did not My hand make all these things?’

relationship: parallel divine regard for a humbled person
rationale: Isaiah says God looks to the humble, quiet person who trembles at His words; the psalm says God will not despise a broken and humbled heart. The psalm places this within its contrast with burnt offerings.
source_text: For My hand made all these things, and all these things are Mine,” says the Lord. “And to whom will I look except the humble and quiet one who trembles at My words?

target_units.text: A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.

relationship: parallel rejection of sacrifice offered by the impious
rationale: Isaiah likens the lawless person's sacrifices to abhorrent acts; Proverbs calls impious people's sacrifices an abomination to the Lord. Isaiah's first comparison is killing a dog, not a substituted killing of a person.
source_text: But the lawless person who sacrifices a calf to Me is like someone killing a dog; the one offering fine flour is like one offering pig’s blood; the one giving frankincense as a memorial is like a blasphemer. These people chose their ways and their abominations, which their soul desired,

target_units.text: The sacrifices of the impious are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those going straight are acceptable to Him.

relationship: close internal repeated charge of ignoring God's call
rationale: Both say God called without obedience, spoke without being heard, and was confronted with chosen evil that He did not want. Their announced punishments differ in expression.
source_text: and I will choose their mockeries and repay their sins to them, because I called them and they did not obey Me, I spoke and they did not hear. They did evil before Me and chose what I did not want.”

target_units.text: I will hand you over to the sword; all of you will fall in slaughter, because I called you and you did not obey, I spoke and you disregarded Me. You did evil before Me and chose what I did not want.”

relationship: related hatred directed toward people attending to God
rationale: Isaiah addresses those trembling at the Lord's word and names those hating and loathing them; Luke blesses disciples hated and excluded because of the Son of Man. The parallel does not resolve Isaiah's further pronouns concerning rejoicing and shame.
source_text: Hear the Lord’s word, you who tremble at His word! Speak, our brothers, to those who hate us and loathe us, so that the Lord’s name may be glorified and seen in their rejoicing; and those people will be ashamed.

target_units.text: Blessed are you when people hate you, when they exclude you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man.

relationship: parallel the Lord's voice sounding from Jerusalem
rationale: Isaiah announces the Lord's recompense in sounds from the city and temple; Amos describes the Lord speaking from Zion and giving His voice from Jerusalem, with the countryside mourning. The venue and divine voice correspond while their effects differ.
source_text: A sound of shouting from the city, a sound from the temple, the sound of the Lord repaying recompense to His opponents!

target_units.text: He said: “The Lord spoke from Zion and gave His voice from Jerusalem; the shepherds’ pastures mourned, and Carmel’s summit dried up.”

relationship: related unexpected children without ordinary labor
rationale: Isaiah 66 describes a woman bearing a male before labor's pain; Isaiah 54 promises many children to the deserted woman who does not labor in childbirth. Both use unexpected childbirth in the restoration imagery, without identical sequences or numbers.
source_text: Before the woman in labor gave birth, before the pain of labor came, she escaped and bore a male.

target_units.text: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth! Break out and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the deserted woman’s children are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband,” for the Lord has spoken.

relationship: parallel Creator's claim over contrasting human bodily conditions
rationale: Isaiah's God asks whether He made both the childbearing woman and the barren woman; Exodus' Lord asks who made people hard of hearing, deaf, seeing or blind. Each rhetorical question attributes people in differing bodily conditions to the Creator, without equating those conditions.
source_text: ‘But I gave this expectation, and you did not remember Me,’ said the Lord. ‘Behold, did I not make the woman who gives birth and the barren woman?’ said God.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Moses, “Who gave a human being a mouth? Who made one hard of hearing or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, God?

relationship: parallel rejoicing over Zion's restoration
rationale: Isaiah calls Jerusalem's lovers and mourners to joy; the psalm recalls Zion's captivity turned back, comfort and mouths filled with joy. The summons and the remembered restoration have different forms.
source_text: Rejoice, Jerusalem, and celebrate in her, all who love her! Rejoice with joy, all who mourn over her,

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. When the Lord turned back Zion’s captivity, we became like those comforted.
Then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Then they will say among the nations, “The Lord has done great things with them.”
The Lord has done great things with us; we became glad.

relationship: internal milk imagery for the city's abundance
rationale: Isaiah 66 depicts people nursing from Jerusalem's comforting breast; Isaiah 60 depicts Jerusalem drinking nations' milk and eating kings' wealth. The city receives abundance in the earlier image and nourishes her people in the later one.
source_text: so that you may nurse and be filled from her comforting breast, so that, nursing fully, you may delight in the entrance of her glory.

target_units.text: You will suck the nations’ milk and eat kings’ wealth. You will know that I am the Lord who saves and delivers you, Israel’s God.

relationship: close internal river imagery associated with peace
rationale: Isaiah 66 says God turns toward them like a river of peace; Isaiah 48 says their peace would have become like a river had they listened. The later declaration differs from the earlier unrealized conditional statement.
source_text: For thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a flooding torrent the glory of nations. Their children will be lifted on shoulders and comforted on knees.

target_units.text: If you had listened to My commands, your peace would have become like a river and your righteousness like a sea wave.

relationship: close children carried on shoulders in the gathering
rationale: Isaiah 66 describes children lifted upon shoulders and comforted on knees; Isaiah 49 describes nations carrying the city's daughters on shoulders. Isaiah 49 distinguishes sons carried in the bosom, while Isaiah 66 uses children collectively.
source_text: For thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a flooding torrent the glory of nations. Their children will be lifted on shoulders and comforted on knees.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “Behold, I lift My hand toward nations and will raise My signal toward islands. They will bring your sons in their bosom and carry your daughters on shoulders,

relationship: complementary parental images for divine care
rationale: Isaiah likens God's comfort to a mother's comfort; the psalm likens His compassion to a father's compassion upon children. The parent and the terms comfort and compassion differ, while both comparisons describe God's care.
source_text: As if a mother were to comfort someone, so I too will comfort you, and in Jerusalem you will be comforted.’

target_units.text: As a father has compassion on children, the Lord had compassion on those who fear Him,

relationship: related rejoicing heart and renewed bodily vigor
rationale: Isaiah joins a rejoicing heart with bones springing up like vegetation; Proverbs says a rejoicing heart makes one flourish and contrasts a sorrowful person's dried bones. The links between inner joy, flourishing and bones are expressed through different contrasts.
source_text: You will see, and your heart will rejoice; your bones will spring up like vegetation. The Lord’s hand will be known to those who revere Him, and He will threaten the disobedient.

target_units.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

relationship: parallel coming in flaming judgment and vengeance
rationale: Isaiah describes the Lord coming like fire to render vengeance; Second Thessalonians describes the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven in flaming fire, bringing vengeance. The letter names the Lord Jesus and His powerful angels, while Isaiah names storm-like chariots.
source_text: For behold, the Lord will come like fire, and His chariots like a storm, to render vengeance in wrath and rejection in a flame of fire.

target_units.text: and to you who are afflicted, relief with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of His power,
in a flame of fire, bringing vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.

relationship: parallel divine blade turned against all flesh
rationale: Isaiah describes all flesh judged by the Lord's sword; Ezekiel describes the Lord drawing His dagger against all flesh and being recognized as its wielder. Ezekiel's stated direction from east to north is not identical to Isaiah's whole-earth scope.
source_text: For by the Lord’s fire all the earth will be judged, and by His sword all flesh; many will be wounded by the Lord.

target_units.text: and say to Israel’s land, ‘Behold, I am against you. I will draw My dagger from its sheath and destroy from you the unjust and the lawless.
Because I will destroy from you the unjust and the lawless, so My dagger will come out of its sheath against all flesh from east to north.
All flesh will recognize that I, the Lord, have drawn My dagger from its sheath, and it will not return again.’

relationship: legal counterpart identifying the mouse among unclean creatures
rationale: Isaiah condemns eating the mouse among abhorrent practices; Leviticus names the mouse among unclean creeping things and gives a rule about touching their dead bodies. The shared classification does not make the legal touching rule identical to Isaiah's eating accusation.
source_text: ‘Those purifying and cleansing themselves for the gardens, eating pig’s flesh and abominations and the mouse in the porches, will be consumed together,’ said the Lord,

target_units.text: And these are unclean for you among the creeping things that creep on the earth: the weasel, the mouse, and the land crocodile;
the shrew, the chameleon, the spotted lizard, the lizard, and the mole.
These are unclean for you among all the creeping things on the earth. Whosoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until evening.

relationship: close gathering of nations and languages around God's presence
rationale: Isaiah promises to gather all nations and languages to see His glory; Zechariah describes many nations seeking the Lord in Jerusalem and people from all nations' languages accompanying a Jew because God is with them. Their descriptions of approach differ.
source_text: ‘and I know their works and their reasoning. I am coming to gather all nations and languages, and they will come and see My glory.

target_units.text: Many peoples and many nations will come to seek the presence of the Lord Almighty in Jerusalem and appease the Lord’s presence.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: In those days, when ten men from all the nations’ languages take hold and grasp the fringe of a Jewish man’s garment, saying, ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you all.’”

relationship: related mission among those not previously hearing the divine message
rationale: Isaiah describes God sending saved people to nations and islands that have not heard His name or seen His glory; Paul describes proclaiming Christ where He was not named and quotes a promise to those who had not heard. The letter's quoted wording is not presented as a verbatim citation of this Isaiah unit.
source_text: I will leave signs upon them and send those saved from them to the nations: to Tharsis, Phoud, Loud, Mosoch, Thobel and Greece, and to the distant islands that have not heard My name or seen My glory. They will announce My glory among the nations.

target_units.text: and so making it my ambition to proclaim the gospel where Christ has not been named, so that I would not build on another’s foundation,
but just as it is written, “Those to whom nothing about Him was announced will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

relationship: related people presented as an offering to God
rationale: Isaiah describes brothers from all nations brought as a gift to the Lord; Paul describes priestly gospel service so the offering of the Gentiles becomes acceptable. Isaiah's transport to Jerusalem and sacrifices with psalms differ from Paul's account of sanctification in the Spirit.
source_text: They will bring your brothers from all nations as a gift to the Lord, with horses and chariots, in mule carriages with sunshades, to the holy city Jerusalem,’ said the Lord, ‘as the Israelites might bring Me their sacrifices with psalms into the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, performing priestly service with God’s gospel, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit.

relationship: internal appointment of people to priestly service
rationale: Isaiah 66 says God will take priests and Levites from them; Isaiah 61 says its addressees will be called priests and ministers of God. The comparison does not settle the precise antecedent of from them in Isaiah 66.
source_text: From them I will take priests and Levites for Myself,’ said the Lord.

target_units.text: But you will be called priests of the Lord, ministers of God. You will consume the nations’ resources and be admired in their wealth.

relationship: internal new-creation promise used to assure enduring descendants
rationale: Isaiah 65 announces new heaven and earth; Isaiah 66 invokes their remaining before God as the comparison for the people's enduring offspring and name. The latter explicitly draws assurance from the creation promise.
source_text: ‘For just as the new heaven and new earth that I make remain before Me,’ says the Lord, ‘so your offspring and your name will stand.

target_units.text: For heaven will be new and earth new, and they will never remember former things, nor will those things enter their heart,

relationship: parallel nations coming to Jerusalem to worship the Lord
rationale: Isaiah promises all flesh worshiping in Jerusalem month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath; Zechariah describes remaining nations coming annually to worship the King, the Lord Almighty. The schedules and descriptions of the worshipers differ.
source_text: Month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath, all flesh will come before Me to bow down in Jerusalem,’ said the Lord.

target_units.text: Whoever remains from all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up each year to bow before the King, the Lord Almighty, and celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.

relationship: close citation of the undying worm and unquenched fire
rationale: Mark's warning about Gehenna repeats the worm not dying and fire not being extinguished. Isaiah describes the transgressors' limbs as a spectacle outside, a detail not repeated in Mark's quoted line.
source_text: ‘They will go out and see the limbs of the people who transgressed against Me, for their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched. They will be a spectacle to all flesh.’

target_units.text: where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.
